value.text: Save the Chimps, a 150-acre chimpanzee sanctuary in Fort Pierce, is asking the community for help after historic flooding left parts of its property underwater, damaged equipment and disrupted normal operations.WATCH REPORT BELOW: The sanctuary's more than 200 chimpanzees are safe and continue to receive food, medication, enrichment and other daily care, according to Mark Yohannan, the organization's director of facilities. But Yohannan told WPTV the sanctuary faces a long recovery after receiving 19 inches of rain."We've got a long way to go," Yohannan said.He said it is the worst flooding the sanctuary has experienced in its 25 years in Fort Pierce."We're absolutely shut down until we get the water gone," Yohannan said.Staff adapts to care for chimpanzeesSince Tuesday, Save the Chimps staff members have had to find new ways to reach parts of the flooded sanctuary. Workers have used tractors and trailers to navigate the property and deliver supplies.Video shared with WPTV shows staff using a drone to drop food to a chimpanzee during the flooding.Despite the difficult conditions, Yohannan said the chimpanzees have continued receiving their normal care."They're doing great. The care staff have been on their game," Yohannan said. "They're getting everything they would get normally: enrichment, all their food, all their medication, blankets. They haven't missed a beat."Yohannan said some staff members have been unable to get to work because of the flooding, but those who can reach the sanctuary have come together to keep operations moving."It's heavy, but it's good heavy," Yohannan said. "Everyone's come together."Flooding damages vehicles and equipmentThe flooding has also taken a toll on equipment used for everyday operations.Yohannan said nearly 15 golf carts used to transport food, supplies and staff around the 150-acre property have broken down."We'd seen the water and we figured, well, no big deal, we'll drive through it, and that became impossible immediately," he said.Yohannan said the sanctuary is looking for taller four-wheel-drive vehicles that can safely move people and supplies through the property while floodwaters remain."We need four-wheel-drive vehicles that are taller that can move supplies and people," Yohannan said. He said the vehicles could be rented or donated for a short period.Save the Chimps asks community for helpAs the sanctuary works to recover, staff members are preparing to bring their concerns to the St. Lucie County Commission at a meeting next week.In the meantime, Save the Chimps is asking the community for support, including temporary access to vehicles and financial donations."A donation goes a long way," Yohannan said.Even as employees deal with challenges at the sanctuary, Yohannan acknowledged that some staff members and Treasure Coast residents are facing flooding problems of their own."There's a lot of people, including our own staff, that have much bigger problems with this water than we have here," he said. "Nobody brings that with them. They just get together, we get to work. We work on that plan, we execute."For a sanctuary that has called Fort Pierce home for 25 years, Yohannan said community support could make a meaningful difference as the water recedes and the recovery continues.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Police are asking for the public's help identifying a driver after a 6-month-old dog was found dead in a Boynton Beach parking lot earlier this week.Shortly after 2:30 p.m. 3, Boynton Beach Police received a report of a dead dog in a parking space at the back of a parking lot at 1500 Southwest 8th Street.WATCH VIDEO BELOW: An animal cruelty officer responded and found a small white dog that appeared to have been run over, according to police.Investigators described the dog as a female Jack Russell Terrier, approximately 6 months old, with white fur and light tan or brown spots.Detectives obtained surveillance video that police said shows a dark-colored sedan, believed to possibly be a Tesla, entering the parking lot at about 1:35 p.m.According to police, the driver parked and got out before walking around the back of the vehicle toward the passenger side. The dog was then seen walking from the passenger side toward the front of the vehicle while the driver walked back around the car and returned to the driver's seat.Police said the dog then walked back toward the passenger side of the vehicle.At about 1:38 p.m., the sedan drove away. The dog was subsequently seen lying motionless on the ground, according to investigators.Police have not identified the driver, and the news release did not specify whether investigators believe the dog was struck intentionally.Detectives are asking anyone who saw anything suspicious near 1500 Southwest 8th Street on Nov. 3, or anyone who recognizes the driver or dog, to contact Detective Sala at 561-742-6818 or SalaN@bbfl.us.

Family, friends and fellow first responders gathered Saturday to say a final goodbye to 34-year-old St. Lucie County firefighter-paramedic Austin Hodge.Hodge, a nine-year veteran of the St. Lucie County Fire District, was remembered for his service to the community and the impact he had on the people around him.WATCH: St. Lucie County firefighter Austin Hodge honored at funeral Saturday"He was somebody who was always ready to help someone," friend Jeff Lewis said on Nov. 6.For Lewis, Hodge's legacy is personal."He leaves this place a better place than he found it. He found you one way but [would] leave you better than he found you."On Oct. Lucie County Fire District said Hodge was found unresponsive in his bunk during a shift change. He was taken to the hospital, where he later died.His unexpected death has been difficult for those closest to him to process."It's a shock to literally all of us," Hodge's sister, Alexis Hodge, said on Oct. 26.She said one of the hardest parts is knowing she can no longer simply call her brother."I love him and I just wish I could pick up the phone and talk to him," Hodge's death comes just over a year after the family suffered another devastating loss. His brother, Jarius Hodge, was also a St. Jarius died in 2025."We've lost two brothers in one year, can't describe to you the pain" Alexis said.On Saturday, an honor guard, a procession and firefighters standing side by side marked a final salute to Hodge and his nine years of service to the St.

Votes are still being counted in Mississippi, in the tight senate race between Democrat Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.Part of the delay in counting is because thousands of voters cast their ballots by affidavit rather than a traditional ballot. Many voters said they were caught by surprise when they learned they would have to vote by affidavit because their registration was marked inactive. “It was very disheartening to be labeled inactive,” voter Kevin Green, a Mississippi voter, told Scripps News this week. “And there was no real rationale behind it.”Green said he has voted consistently since moving back to his home state of Mississippi in 2020. He said he received a notice from the NAACP telling him to look up his registration status in the days before the election. When he did, he was shocked to see his status was inactive. After speaking to the county clerk, he learned he would have to vote by affidavit because he had not responded to a mailer seeking to verify his address. After successfully voting on Election Day by affidavit, Green posted about his experience on social media. “We know there was some shady business going on there,” Green told Scripps News, pointing to the state’s history of disenfranchising Black voters. “It's really not a good look for our state when we've come so far, and the fact that this election is now so close speaks volumes about where we've come.”Ralph Sandidge said he was disappointed to find out he had been purged from the voter rolls when he arrived to cast his ballot this year.“I said, ‘Well, who did that? Under what authority?’” Sandidge said. Sandidge said he was told he was no longer registered to vote because he had not voted in several elections. Election experts told Scripps News the large number of inactive voters this election in Mississippi may be due in part to the state’s reliance on consumer data provided by Experian to maintain its voter rolls. The state used the data to check voter addresses, but experts said the data may have contained errors affecting thousands of voters. “Everything we've heard from the Secretary of State's office is that this was a good faith effort to keep the voter rolls accurate,” said Daniel Griffith, the senior director of policy at Secure Democracy. “Because it wasn't based on the best practices, and because the credit agency data is not reliable, it has had an unfortunate outcome for a lot of individuals.”Thomas Minor said he encountered such an error when he attempted to vote in the primary election earlier this year. He told Scripps News the clerk told him his registration was inactivated because Experian data said he lived in another city. However, he told Scripps News, he has not moved for a decade. He was able to fix the error and vote normally during the general election on Tuesday but was dismayed to see so many other voters encounter the same problem he had months ago. “It feels like somebody’s trying to pull strings somewhere and mess things up,” Minor said. “We have no evidence that there is something sinister (happening), and election officials are very, very careful and very committed to protect elections and not disenfranchise voters,” said Thessalia Merivaki, a distinguished professor of government at Washington State University. “Sometimes your data are bad, and this is what happens.”An Experian spokesperson said its company has not provided services to the state since 2025.“The solution provided at that time consisted of supplemental address information and was not designed or intended to validate voter records,” said Scott Anderson, vice president of corporate communications for Experian, in a statement sent Friday to Scripps News. “Decisions regarding voter registration policies, procedures and record updates are made solely by election officials in accordance with applicable local, state and federal laws.”The Mississippi Secretary of State’s Office did not respond to multiple voice messages and emails from Scripps News.RELATED STORY | Democrat clings to razor-thin lead in Mississippi Senate raceIn a Friday interview with Democracy Docket, Colom criticized the state for its use of Experian data and said voters experiencing ballot problems should contact his campaign for help. Merivaki said she expects the Secretary of State’s office will investigate what went wrong. In the meantime, election clerks across Mississippi are counting affidavit ballots to determine the winners of Tuesday’s election. Voters who provided identification and voted by affidavit do not need to take any further action for their votes to be counted. Those who did not have ID with them have until Tuesday to rectify their affidavits. The Secretary of State’s office posted a tracker online for voters who voted absentee or by affidavit to ensure their ballot is being counted.Kevin Green said he’s happy to know his vote will count, but wants the process to change going forward. “Obviously there are some gaps there, and we need to revisit that and ensure that we have effective policies that are in place,” he said.

Nearly a week after a Learjet crash killed nine people in Greenacres and forced hundreds from their homes, some residents are still waiting for an answer to the question that has consumed their lives since the crash.For those who haven't been allowed to return, the cost of being displaced is adding up.WATCH REPORT BELOW: "When are they going to let us back home?" Joseph Santana Quiroz asked WPTV.He hasn't been allowed home all week.He told WPTV he has also had to miss work without pay."If you can't work, they can't pay you?" WPTV reporter Joel Lopez asked."Exactly," Santana Quiroz said.But even without a paycheck, the bills don't stop."We can't tell the bank we can't pay because this happened," Santana Quiroz said.He is one of 31 people still sheltering at the Greenacres Community Center as the investigation continues.Now, organizations are stepping in to help with everything from those immediate financial pressures to the challenges residents could face when they are finally allowed back home.The Emergency Assistance Foundation, a West Palm Beach-based nonprofit, launched the People First Fund for Green Acres Mobile Home Community Learjet Crash to provide direct financial assistance to eligible residents impacted by the crash."We actually are ready and prepared to start taking in grant applications at this time," said Josselyn Hodges, director of the People First Fund Initiative at Emergency Assistance Foundation.She told WPTV the organization normally responds to disasters and hardships around the world, but this time the need is close to home."We are a global public charity that does financial assistance to impacted individuals after disasters around the world. However, we're headquartered here in West Palm Beach, so we felt compelled to help our neighbors," Hodges said.The organization plans to provide $1,000 cash grants to eligible individuals, allowing residents to decide where that money is needed most."Our goal is to be able to provide that financial assistance so people can take care of their most urgent self-assessed needs," Hodges said. "We understand that when people get displaced from their homes, they experience financial hardship in seeking temporary housing, in seeking food and other personal hardships."Hodges said the cash assistance is intended to complement the food, shelter and other services being provided by different organizations."While there may be other organizations that support with food or housing, this financial assistance and cash assistance that will be, landing directly into the hands of individuals is meant to be able to help those individuals, take, buy supplies or take care of whatever items are, heaviest in their mind at this time," Hodges said.Through donations from community foundations and individual donors, Hodges said the fund currently has enough money to provide $1,000 grants to 18 people.But the organization wants to go further."We understand that there are about 68 impacted individuals from the mobile home community, the Green Acres mobile home community, so we are calling on to the community to come together and be able to, turn that compassion into tangible support and help us reach every single one of these members," Hodges said.Hodges said the goal is to raise enough money to provide a grant to all 68 individuals the organization has identified.Residents looking for assistance won't simply have to navigate the process on their own. Hodges said EAF is working with members of the Emergency Operations Center to identify people with the greatest needs and provide them with a direct link to apply.For residents who don't know when they'll be able to return home, Hodges said the goal is to provide some immediate relief while other assistance is still coming together."We believe in the power of community. We know that people wanna come together and help community members in the wake of hardships and disasters, so we have a way to be able to provide that immediate impact now while other resources are still mobilizing," Hodges said. "That is our goal, to be able to support people in the very first critical days of their recovery process."Preparing for what happens when residents return homeThe financial fallout may not end when people are finally able to return.State Rep. Debra Tendrich is working through her organization, Eat Better Live Better, to prepare for another expense some families could face: replacing spoiled food."If you look at what's happening with their electricity being cut off and the power grid shut down, you're looking at people returning to their homes and having to throw out their entire refrigerator full of food that they might have just purchased or or that they need to fill now," Tendrich said.For families already dealing with displacement and lost income, Tendrich wants to make replacing those groceries one less thing they have to worry about."I'm really working right now to make sure that we are able to help fill those refrigerators," Tendrich said.Tendrich's nonprofit operates an affordable farmers market-style food pantry with fresh and healthy items.She said her organization was already seeing an increased demand for grocery assistance before the crash."We, we've been seeing an increased need as is. My organization has received between 25 and 100 new applications every week needing grocery assistance," Tendrich said. "So to pile that up with having to now, have your entire refrigerator needs to be thrown out and then also replenish that just doubles down on how hard times are right now for my community."For Tendrich, it's about helping families move toward some sense of normalcy after days of uncertainty."The last thing that you want to worry about is how are you going to feed yourself, your family and your children after a tragedy like this," Tendrich said.Tendrich said displaced families are also dealing with needs that can easily be overlooked during a prolonged evacuation, including getting to doctor's appointments and accessing medications."Families with their children are trying to get to doctor's appointments, get their medications that they need, uh, we're really trying to make sure that people are accessing everything they need at this moment to get through this while they're displaced from their homes," Tendrich said. "We're doing everything we can between the county, the police, the fire and my office. We're working hard to make sure not only while you're, you're displaced, but once you get back home, we're trying to make sure that you're supported as much as possible during this, this tough time."While groups are getting to work countywide, help continues while families wait as other organizations are addressing needs at the shelter itself.Many other organizations like the Red Cross, and community members have dropped off supplies this week.Dare to Care has been providing mobile showers and laundry services at the Greenacres Community Center."They called us on Monday and said, ‘Can you come out?’ We've been here ever since," said Timothy Murphy, with the organization Dare to Care. "My message to residents is that there are people who care. We're here for those in need no matter what," he said. "When crisis happen it just complies, so we're here to relieve some of the loss."It remains unclear how long all of the impacted residents will be displaced.Click here if you'd like to help make monetary donations.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Our editorial team verifies all reporting on all platforms for fairness and accuracy.

Five days after a Learjet crashed into Military Trail, killing all nine people on board, the father of a 20-year-old co-pilot is breaking his silence, sharing his grief publicly for the first time and vowing to preserve his daughter's legacy."She was gifted. She was gifted, and my soulmate," Allan Filgueiras said Friday, fighting back tears as he remembered his daughter, Nathalia Filgueiras.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Nathalia was one of nine people killed Sunday when the aircraft crashed into Military Trail near 10th Avenue North in Greenacres, leaving a crater in the roadway and scattering debris across nearby homes and businesses. A driver on the ground was also injured.Five days later, wreckage remained at the scene as investigators continued working to determine what caused the crash.For Nathalia's father, the search for answers is deeply personal. But he wants the world to remember his daughter not for how she died, but for how she lived.Standing alongside his attorneys Friday, Filgueiras spoke publicly about his daughter's life, her love of aviation and the final moments he has replayed in his mind since the crash.His attorney, Stuart Grossman of Grossman, Yaffa & Cohen, said the family has retained legal counsel but has not filed a lawsuit."It is customary among law firms that the moment they file a lawsuit, to call a press conference," Grossman said. "This is not today's topic. We're suing no one yet."Instead, Grossman said the family wanted to express its condolences to the other eight families grieving loved ones and thank the National Transportation Safety Board for its ongoing investigation."We're not making allegations against anybody at this time," Grossman said. "We're going to do the right thing, and we're going to listen to what the government uncovers. Then we'll have our experts look at it and say they agree or not."But Grossman said the family's decision to speak publicly also serves another purpose: protecting Nathalia's reputation."The purpose of this is to preserve not just her memory but her reputation," Grossman said. "Nathalia was beyond an average pilot; she was extraordinary."Despite her young age, Grossman said Nathalia was highly trained and qualified to serve as co-pilot."She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years," he said.Grossman also addressed questions about how someone so young could be flying a jet."When you read that someone's 20 years old, and a co-pilot in a jet plane, you say, 'How can this be?'" Grossman said. "Well, wait until you see her hours, and what the government proves about her capabilities and what her instructors had to say."He described her death as a loss not only to her family but to the aviation community."This is a loss to aviation," Grossman said.Long before Nathalia was flying jets, she was a 12-year-old girl discovering her passion for aviation alongside her father.Allan, a pilot himself, introduced his daughter to flying before she was old enough to drive.Grossman said that the early bond between father and daughter made the tragedy even more painful."My client Allan, who is her father, was the reason why she flew," Grossman said. "From the time she was 12 years old, she, who was a pilot, Allan would take her up, and she fell in love with flying."As Nathalia grew older, that childhood passion became her career.Her father recalled how she would marvel at being paid to do something she loved so much."She said, 'Dad, can you believe? Can you believe that I would pay for this, but they're actually paying me,'" Filgueiras recalled. "It was her happiest moment to fly." Eventually, the roles between father and daughter reversed. Allan, who had once taught Nathalia to fly, found himself learning from her."When we were flying together, I used to instruct her, but then she became my instructor," he said. Now, the same father who taught Nathalia to fly is struggling to understand how her life ended.Filgueiras said he has listened repeatedly to air traffic control recordings from the aircraft's final moments, searching for answers. "I did listen to that many times, trying to find a clue in my head how that happened," he said. "And wow, she's tough."He said hearing his daughter's final moments left him proud of her determination."She made me so proud," Filgueiras said. "She showed me what it is to be a hero."The NTSB has not yet determined the cause of the crash. Investigators are examining the circumstances surrounding the aircraft's final flight.Grossman said the family's legal team intends to wait for the federal investigation before reaching its own conclusions."We'll let you know when the report comes out what our point of view is on it," he said.The attorney also acknowledged the families on the ground whose homes and lives were disrupted by the crash, expressing sympathy for those displaced while investigators continue their work.For now, Filgueiras is focused on remembering his daughter and finding a way forward for his wife and surviving children.Speaking partly in Spanish, he described the loss as having his heart ripped from his chest.He said he knows he must find a way to keep going for his family — and for Nathalia. "Nathalia doesn't want to see a father falling apart," he said in Spanish. "So I gotta — I'm gonna find a way. I'm gonna find a way to make her proud."He also recalled their spontaneous flights together, traveling to places like Key West and Naples just to grab a cup of coffee or something to eat.Those simple moments are now memories he will carry for the rest of his life.And while some families grieve privately, Filgueiras chose to share his heartbreak in front of cameras Friday — not to assign blame, but to honor the daughter he wishes he could have protected.When Investigative Reporter Kate Hussey asked what he would say to Nathalia if he could speak to her again, the grieving father broke down."I wanted to be by her side. To be by her teammates," he said through tears. "I had to be next to her."For a father who spent years sharing the skies with his daughter, it is the one flight he wishes he could have taken with her.The NTSB's investigation into the crash remains ongoing. No cause has yet been determined.

A new elementary school in Westlake is quickly taking shape, with project leaders saying construction remains on time and on budget despite recent heavy rain and flooding.WPTV reporter Christy Waite first toured the construction site in August, when much of the school was still a concrete slab. She returned to the site on Friday and found a much different scene, with the building now taking shape.WATCH REPORT BELOW:Site Superintendent Brad Stapleton said recent weather created challenges for crews, with parts of the construction site underwater."We joked that we should have brought kayaks and canoes to work to get from our trailer and parking to the building because a lot of this area that we are standing in now was underwater," Stapleton said.Despite those conditions, Stapleton said construction has stayed on track."We are looking great for meeting the August turnover for the next school year," he said.Principal Darline Winewski has watched the school rise from the ground up and said seeing the individual spaces inside the building is making the project feel more real."To actually see the walls come up and really be able to see the individual spaces, I'm just so excited," Winewski said.As Westlake continues to grow, the $48 million school will have room for 972 students in pre-K through fifth grade.Winewski said the new school will fill a need for families whose children currently attend two different schools."We really have a need for this school in our community. Our families deserve that. They are going to two different schools right now," Winewski said.Waite also connected with parent Krystal Lexima, whose daughter is looking forward to the new school opening."She's so excited to walk the halls for the first time," Lexima said.Another milestone is coming soon. The school's official name, mascot and colors are expected to be revealed next month."We submitted our names to the board and we will find out soon enough and start identifying ourselves officially," Winewski said.

Nine people lost their lives when a Learjet crashed into Military Trail in Greenacres on Sunday. But the devastation extends beyond those on board, leaving at least one family on the ground without access to their home, their business and the life they knew before the crash.Now, that family has hired an attorney to investigate what went wrong and determine whether anyone could be held legally responsible.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Ricardo Martinez-Cid, a partner at Miami law firm Podhurst Orseck, told WPTV his clients were inside the area impacted by the crash when debris struck, injuring family members and sending them to the hospital.Their home was damaged and remains inaccessible. Their food truck, which they relied on for their livelihood, was also lost."We want to be really sensitive in talking about how this has impacted their lives because it's been horrific for them," Martinez-Cid said. "But they're sensitive to the fact that nine people lost their lives on board that aircraft, and this is a horrible tragedy."Martinez-Cid said the family is now grappling with the emotional and financial consequences of a disaster they never saw coming."Although my clients, you know, lost their home, they lost their livelihood in the food truck that they operated. They were injured and went to the hospital, and they're dealing with the trauma of what they witnessed and experienced," he said. "They're lucky; they're blessed because nine folks lost their lives."Martinez-Cid, a board-certified aviation attorney with more than two decades of experience, said his firm is conducting its own investigation into the crash.The goal is to determine what caused the Learjet to go down and whether any individual, company or other entity bears legal responsibility."You don't want to jump to conclusions," Martinez-Cid said. "But in every aviation disaster ... you're really looking at man, the machine and the environment."That means examining several potential factors, including weather conditions, pilot decisions, air traffic control communications and the aircraft's mechanical performance."We're looking at the weather, we're looking at the piloting, we're looking at how the aircraft responds, we're looking at the communications between the tower and with the pilots," he said. "We're going to look very closely at how the aircraft responded to what was going on as well."Martinez-Cid said his firm has previously handled aviation cases involving aircraft manufacturers, pilots, operators and the federal government."I've tried cases against the United States government on air traffic control weather instructions on the sufficiency of them," he said. "We've also done plenty of cases ... against Lears, specifically Cessna and the manufacturers, to determine if there was any structural issue or any mechanical issue with the aircraft."While investigators have not determined what caused Sunday's crash, Martinez-Cid said publicly available information has already provided several areas worth examining."With the data that has already been publicly available, which includes a lot of the communications and what we know about the weather already, there's a lot to look at and investigate in this case," he said.No conclusions about liability have been reached, and Martinez-Cid did not identify a specific party his clients intend to pursue legal action against.The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the federal investigation into the crash, but Martinez-Cid said families may need independent experts to evaluate the evidence and explore potential legal claims."Unfortunately, the NTSB process can be very slow," he said. "And also the conclusions of the NTSB are not usable in any action in court. So families need to get their own answers."Martinez-Cid said his firm plans to work with aviation experts to independently analyze available data, including communications, weather information and the aircraft's performance."So we look at it from all angles, and we make sure our experts get all the data that they can," he said.Martinez-Cid confirmed his firm has also been in contact with attorneys connected to families of people killed aboard the Learjet."We've been contacted by, which is often the case, attorneys that either are friends with the family or have been contacted by the family because of our expertise globally on these issues," he said. "And so we've been speaking to some."He said those conversations are not necessarily limited to potential lawsuits."We have experts that can talk to the families and explain the different things that they're hearing and what's going on, and I think that's an important thing for the family to have."Martinez-Cid previously served as lead counsel for death and injury cases stemming from the 2021 Champlain Towers South condominium collapse in Surfside.He said that experience reinforced the importance of recognizing the different kinds of losses families endure after a disaster.For the family Martinez-Cid represents in Greenacres, the immediate future remains uncertain.Their home is inaccessible, their source of income is gone, and they are recovering from injuries and the trauma of witnessing a deadly plane crash.Martinez-Cid declined to identify the family, saying they are still struggling emotionally with the aftermath.But he emphasized that while his clients recognize how fortunate they are to have survived, their lives have been permanently changed."Their life has been turned upside down," he said. "They're going to be living with this trauma forever. They've lost their livelihood."Still, he said the family remains deeply aware of the grief experienced by those who lost loved ones."Their hearts really go out to those who have lost loved ones," Martinez-Cid said.He hopes the investigation will eventually provide answers for everyone affected by the crash, regardless of whether they were aboard the plane or on the ground."They all suffer loss, and you have to respect each individual family member, and you have to respect each individual case and treat them all with the care and the respect that they deserve," he said.The NTSB investigation remains ongoing, and the cause of the crash has not been determined.

A longtime organizer of Lake Worth Beach’s Día de Muertos festival is bringing the celebration to West Palm Beach this weekend after this year's Lake Worth Beach event was canceled.Local artist and educator Jose R. Mendez will host Día de Muertos at The Peach on Saturday from 3 p.m. at The Peach arts collective, 3950 Georgia Ave. Admission is free, and the event is open to the public.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Mendez co-founded the original Día de Muertos celebration in Lake Worth Beach in 2016 and helped develop and coordinate the festival for years. He said he organized Saturday’s independent event because he did not want the local tradition to disappear."I do not want to see a tradition that I helped create, that has become so meaningful to our community, come to an end," Mendez said.This year's celebration also carries a personal significance for Mendez. Mendez, recently died in Guatemala."Part of the reason I moved forward with this was to honor my dad, who passed away a couple of weeks ago," Mendez said. "He was big on culture."Saturday’s celebration will feature traditional Día de Muertos ofrendas, or altars, along with local artisan vendors, face painting, outdoor art installations and a children’s activity zone presented by Raices Creative Arts Academy.The entertainment lineup includes Mariachi De Mi Tierra Internacional, vocalist Emmanuel Gonzalez, a Selena tribute by Liz Ramirez and a performance by Latinos A Bailar, a dance group from John I. Leonard High School.Catrin and Catrina costume contests will also be held for adults, children and pets. Food and drinks will be available from El Segundo, the restaurant located at The Peach.Organizers say this year’s event will be smaller than previous celebrations in Lake Worth Beach, which attracted as many as 6,000 people."I'm not the kind of guy that likes to scale back," Mendez said. "But I believe bringing even one-quarter of our audience to a new location would be a significant step toward keeping this tradition alive."Mendez helped coordinate Lake Worth Beach’s Día de Muertos celebrations from 2016 through 2024. His work has focused on public art, cultural research and creating opportunities for people of different ages to participate in the arts.Organizers said the goal of Saturday's event remains the same despite the new location: creating a place where families can celebrate and share cultural traditions across generations.

Recent flooding has displaced residents and wildlife, with animals appearing in unfamiliar areas. In Indian River County, floodwaters also pushed an alligator out of its usual habitat and into a residential driveway. On Friday, the Indian River County Sheriff's Office was on the scene, safely removing the animal from the residence and relocated it to a more suitable area within the county. No one was hurt, and the alligator was unharmed. Body camera video shows Indian River County deputies approaching what appears to be a huge gator. As they capture the critter, video shows the gator thrashing and hissing before deputies get it into a caged van. The video continues to show deputies releasing the alligator back into the wild. See also: Flooded roads force detours for drivers, but offer wildlife a shortcu t On Thursday, CBS12 crews were covering residential flooding in Port St. Lucie and were told to leave after alligators were confirmed in the streets. An otter was also spotted after the flooding. Martin County officials shared video showing the animal navigating the changed landscape.

Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. A viral video showing a student swimming home from a school bus in flooded Port St. Lucie streets has raised questions about why schools opened during Monday’s severe weather. The video, filmed in a neighborhood where water has since receded, shows the student navigating deep floodwaters after exiting the bus. "He literally almost went completely underwater," said Lucinda Lopez, a Port St. Another neighbor, Ariel Abel, described the scene: "We watched the school bus get stuck over in that turn area, and then we watched the kid get off, and he sunk straight into the water." The incident has left parents questioning why schools opened on Monday despite the flooding. Concerns include why buses were sent into severely flooded streets and whether students should have sheltered in place at school until conditions improved. "Seeing the danger that all of the kids were put in is not okay," Lopez said. Abel added, "They really dropped the ball on this. The community is disappointed." On Tuesday, St. Lucie Public Schools Superintendent Dr. Jon Prince addressed the situation during a news conference, apologizing to families for the district’s response. The first flood advisory for the county came in just after 8 a.m. Monday, with the first flash flood warning issued at 10:41 a.m. "I completely understand the frustration families feel," Prince said. "It caused a lot of stress for our families, and for that, I’m profoundly sorry." Despite the apology, some parents remain unsatisfied. "An apology doesn’t fix what is happening," Abel said. Lopez emphasized the need for change: "We need to do better. We need to protect our kids at all costs. Missing a day or two of school is okay if it means keeping our kids safe at all costs." WPBF is working to hear from the school district to address these concerns and questions. Floodwaters continue to inundate properties in Martin County, leaving cattle farmers struggling to care for their animals and residents concerned about how much longer the water will remain. Residents in the Trailside community say water from neighboring properties is flowing into their drainage system, causing widespread flooding. Flooding threatens cattle, farm operations Hungryland Farms normally operates a 20-acre rotational grazing system for its Florida Cracker cattle. The owner, Melissa, said much of the pasture is now underwater, forcing the animals onto the farm’s elevated driveway. "We're starting to lose big sections of the driveway. We have them concentrated up the house pad, but if we lose too much more, we're just going to have to figure out a way to evacuate them somewhere," she said. Some cattle have struggled to navigate the water, and Melissa said the farm is concerned about losing access to its property as flooding continues. For now, the farm is bringing in hay and hay cubes to keep the cattle on their regular diet while monitoring potential health risks from floodwaters. "We’re more just concerned with the health and safety of our cattle," Melissa said. Melissa said the farm has an emergency contact with the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Natural Resources Conservation Service if the animals face imminent danger. "We don’t know how long we’re going to be here," she said. HOA says solution is unclear Kyla Shay, president of the Trailside Homeowners Association, said the community’s drainage system is designed to handle water from its 41 lots and designated neighboring properties. However, Shay said water from outside that system is now flowing through county-owned land and other neighboring properties before reaching the community’s southern canal. We can’t handle theirs," Shay said. The flooding has also affected neighboring pastures and reached areas near Bridge Road and an electrical substation, according to Shay. She said some electrical transformers are partially underwater, septic systems are overwhelmed and residents have been warned their well water could be compromised. "The health department issued warnings this morning to me that our water wells could be compromised because of bacteria, because of the standing water," Shay said. Since their septic systems are submerged, Shay said homeowners have been unable to shower or do laundry. County says repairs must wait WPBF 25 News reached out to Martin County about their concerns and learned the county recently acquired approximately 315 acres of land in the area, known as the Elise J. A county spokesperson said establishing access has been their immediate priority so staff can assess conditions and respond. The county said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District to address a breach affecting drainage into its irrigation canal and that the agencies jointly determined repairs should wait until water levels recede. The county said current conditions make hauling and placing sand unsafe and potentially damaging to the levee. Material could also wash into the canal before crews establish a stable repair. "County staff will continue to monitor water levels and site conditions in close coordination with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District," a county spokesperson said. The county said it will move forward with repairs when conditions allow safe work without compromising the levee. It is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce the risk of flooding happening again. Residents want a long-term solution Shay said the homeowners association has been working with water engineers and other experts to understand how long the flooding could last. "It's probably going to be late January, February before we can see a break, and that's assuming that the south canal wall does not collapse and immediately dump all the water on us," she said. Melissa said the farm’s drainage system normally provides room for water to collect during the rainy season, but the amount coming from outside the property has overwhelmed it. "We have a very extensive drainage system, but it’s just not equipped to handle this amount of water," Melissa said. Both women said they want neighboring properties and the agencies responsible for drainage to address the problem. For now, Martin County said it will continue monitoring conditions and coordinating with the conservancy district before attempting repairs. Meanwhile, Melissa said the farm is focused on keeping its cattle safe as water continues to surround the property.

With a very strong El Niño event in the Pacific, the U.S. weather pattern is significantly impacted, especially in winter. Historically, El Niño brings stormier weather for the southern United States, including Florida.According to the National Weather Service (NWS) Miami, above-normal rainfall is anticipated for our dry season with a higher risk for flood events and severe weather including tornadoes.This happens as El Niño drives the subtropical jet stream farther south across the U.S. during the winter and dry season and generally steers more storm systems eastward.The NWS says due to the strength of the El Niño, which could match or exceed the historic 1997–1998 event as the strongest recorded (since 1950), confidence is high for a higher risk of strong storms. The 1997-1998 El Niño is tied to multiple severe weather events and the deadliest tornado outbreak in Florida back in February of '98. AFFECT ON WINTER TEMPERATURESAlthough more storm systems are in the forecast, it doesn't mean we will necessarily see more cold snaps or days with freezing temperatures. Because the dominant subtropical jet stream drives more southern storm systems, cold air masses from the north rarely penetrate into Florida. This lowers, but does not completely eliminate the overall likelihood of extreme cold events.The NWS forecasts near-average temperatures for South Florida as more frequent storm systems tends to depress daily high temperatures, while streams of milder Pacific air keep overnight lows higher than normal.IMPACT ON DROUGHT AND WILDFIRESDue to these moist conditions, significant wildfire activity is projected to remain below normal through the winter and potentially extending into the spring.

Friends of 18-year-old Kenneth "Kenny" Donahue are mourning the Spanish River High School senior after he was killed in an e-bike crash on West Palmetto Park Road in Boca Raton, just hours after spending Halloween night with friends.Donahue's friends told WPTV reporter Zitlali Solache they are struggling with the sudden loss while remembering the plans they had made together, including attending college.Watch report from Zitlali Solache:A blue cross now marks the area along West Palmetto Park Road where the crash occurred."That's where it happened, so it deserves to be known," said Sawyer Geldert, a close friend of Kenny.The memorial is a place for Donahue's loved ones to remember the 18-year-old they describe as funny, loving, optimistic and caring."I still text him," Geldert said. "It hurts to lose someone so close to you. And if I could see him one last time, I would hug him and never let go."The Boca Raton Police Services Department said its Traffic Homicide Unit is investigating the crash, which happened shortly before 2 a.m. on West Palmetto Park Road between Interstate 95 and Military Trail.According to police, the driver of a 2025 blue Corvette was traveling east on West Palmetto Park Road when the car struck an electric bicycle carrying two people.Police said Donahue was the passenger on the e-bike and suffered fatal injuries. He was pronounced dead at the scene.Police said the 16-year-old operating the e-bike was taken to a hospital and was listed in stable condition. The Corvette driver was not injured.Investigators are evaluating whether criminal charges will be filed in Donahue's death.Friends told WPTV they had spent Halloween night with Donahue before learning hours later that he had been killed."I was speechless," Rafaella Gonzalez said. "I couldn't even feel any emotions in the moment. I was just so devastated."As they grieve, Donahue's friends are focusing on the person they knew."The funny, loving, always optimistic, caring person that you would see every single day," Kazim Raza said.Santiago Rocha said his friend left an impact on those around him."I also feel Kenny was sent from God to teach us about how to love each other," Rocha said.For Donahue's classmates, his absence is especially noticeable at Spanish River High School."I miss being able to give him the hugs I gave him every day," London Adams said. "I miss the way he smelled. I miss the way he laughed. He was genuinely such an important person to all of us. It's really hard for it to be so quiet in school now."Donahue's friends said the loss has also forced them to confront a future they expected him to be part of."We were literally talking about it the night before, where we were going to college together," said Geldert. "I was supposed to dorm with him."Loved ones said Donahue enjoyed sports, working out and spending time with other people. They said he wanted to become a police officer and serve people.Melonie James, who identified herself as a close friend of Donahue's mother, told WPTV that watching his mother grieve has been heartbreaking."She won't get to see her baby graduate," James said.Friends said the 16-year-old who was operating the e-bike is recovering."He's doing well," Hudson Quinonez said. "I'm so glad he's OK because it could've been so much worse."As the investigation continues, Donahue's loved ones are asking anyone who saw what happened to come forward so they can better understand the circumstances surrounding his death."We just need to piece together the night," said James. "We need help."Loved ones have created the email address info@justiceforkenny.com for information about the crash.The Boca Raton Police Services Department is also asking witnesses or anyone with information about the investigation to contact Officer Gonzalez at 561-419-4124. Donahue is expected to be laid to rest Friday.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Lucie County is asking residents, businesses and agricultural property owners affected by recent flooding to report damage through an online survey as officials work to document the extent of the impacts.The survey is open to property owners and tenants across the county, including Fort Pierce, Port St. Lucie Village and unincorporated St. Lucie County.WATCH REPORT BELOW:County officials said the information collected will be shared with local, state and federal partners to help assess the extent of the flooding and guide recovery efforts.The survey asks respondents to provide the property's location and building type, along with basic information about flooding and damage. It also includes questions about private wells used for household water and septic systems.People can complete the flood impact survey here through Friday, Nov. 20.WATCH: Heavy rains flood Port St. Lucie roads earlier this weekCounty officials stressed that completing the survey is not an application for assistance and does not guarantee that funding will be available. WPTV is working to get answers about how Palm Beach County leaders are responding to historic rainfall that has left neighborhoods underwater, stranded drivers and forced dozens of rescues.The flooding comes during an extraordinary stretch for Palm Beach County, with emergency crews simultaneously responding to flooding, the deadly plane crash near Military Trail and disruptions surrounding Election Day.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Palm Beach County's Emergency Operations Center is operating at Level 2, a partial activation, as county agencies coordinate their response to the flooding and plane crash.Gov. Ron DeSantis expanded Florida's state of emergency Wednesday to include Palm Beach County. The declaration gives state and local officials additional authority and resources for response, recovery and mitigation efforts.County commissioners are now weighing in on the flooding and what they’ve seen in their communities."This rain, my gosh, it never ends," Commissioner Maria Sachs said.Commissioner Gregg Weiss pointed to the extraordinary rainfall totals in parts of West Palm Beach."Parts of West Palm Beach received over 22 inches of rain," Weiss said. "These were epic amounts of water that came down very quickly."Weiss described the rainfall as the kind of extreme event some characterize as a "one-in-1,000-type" storm. He also acknowledged that some residents will be dealing with the consequences long after the rain stops."I know in some of our eastern areas their homes received water inside, so there’s going to be work to do there," Weiss said.For Sachs, the flooding is also raising a larger question about how Palm Beach County prepares for future growth.She pointed to the importance of planning for drainage when new homes and businesses are built."I know our aquifers can take only so much," Sachs said. "When we develop residences and commercial properties, we develop them with the idea of drainage."The flooding has turned roads into waterways, stranded vehicles and left some residents unable to get out of their neighborhoods.Among those who were affected was Commissioner Bobby Powell Jr., who represents Palm Beach County Commission District 7."There's people in my community that were not able to go to work," Powell said.Powell told commissioners that he experienced the flooding firsthand."Fire Rescue came to get me this morning, so I'm one of the people they had to rescue," Powell said.Palm Beach County Fire Rescue told WPTV its crews conducted multiple flood response operations from Sunday through Tuesday.Sunday night, firefighters responded to more than seventy 911 calls in the Century Village area near West Palm Beach. Nearly 100 residents were trapped in stranded vehicles as floodwaters rapidly rose.WATCH BELOW: Flooding in Century VillageFirefighters reported encountering floating cars with people still inside and water reaching between 3 and 4 feet deep in some areas.Crews deployed drones equipped with thermal imaging cameras around Century Village, Cypress Lakes, the Tennis Club and other areas to search vehicles for people who needed help.Firefighters then waded through the water and used high-water vehicles and brush trucks to rescue residents and bring them to higher ground.Fire Rescue said there were no injuries during those operations.Palm Beach County Fire Rescue's Urban Search and Rescue Swiftwater Response Team was also deployed to Riviera Beach for nearly 24 hours.With some streets impassable, rescue specialists used emergency rafts and boats to go door to door.Fire Rescue said its teams:Evacuated 71 peopleConducted two medical rescuesEvacuated nine petsCounty officials have continued reporting significant impacts from the flooding in Riviera Beach and other communities.PBCFR said from Nov. 1-3, crews responded to a total of more than 1,600 emergency calls across the county. This figure included all 911 calls, not just flooding.The flooding wasn't the only major emergency stretching Palm Beach County's resources.At the same time, fire rescue crews were carrying out flood response operations; dozens of personnel and resources were also dedicated to the deadly Learjet crash near Greenacres.The crash also displaced an estimated 400 to 600 people from a nearby mobile home community. WPTV spoke with residents who were unable to return to their homes, vehicles and belongings while investigators worked through the crash scene.The county then opened an emergency shelter where some residents have been ever since."We've been communicating with our municipalities, making sure we have shelters, that we have anything needed to address the concerns of our families," said Commissioner Joel Flores, adding Election Day presented another challenge as he noted three precincts had to be moved because of all the flooding.Vice Mayor Marci Woodward pointed to the strain of responding to both disasters at once."We had a horrific plane crash and also ended up with flooding, so to all the employees that have worked a lot of long hours, I wanted to personally thank all of you, and I know our residents appreciate all the efforts, so thank you for that," Woodward said.State of emergency now includes Palm Beach CountyThe county’s response is continuing with the state now involved in recovery efforts.DeSantis amended Florida's existing flooding emergency order Wednesday to add Palm Beach County along with Glades, Hendry, Lake, Okeechobee, Seminole and Volusia counties.The Florida Division of Emergency Management said the move strengthens the state's ability to deploy resources, support local response efforts and help communities recover.The emergency declaration also gives state and local officials additional authority to carry out response, recovery and mitigation efforts, including logistical, rescue and evacuation operations. Local governments can waive certain procedures involving public works, contracts, equipment, workers and spending when necessary to speed up the emergency response.If you're in need of flooding emergency, call 2-1-1.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. The passing of Amendment 3 has now put Florida cities on notice to find ways to handle the anticipated loss of revenue."I was interviewed a couple of years ago when this first came up, and I said, 'What are we going to do, have a bake sale,' and here we are," says Lake Worth Beach Mayor Betty Resch.WATCH REPORT BELOW: According to Florida Tax Watch, Lake Worth Beach stands to lose $2.9 million in the first year of the higher homestead exemption and $5 million in the second year."We can't just keep raising the fees. We can't charge somebody if they want to go to the library," Resch said.Voters made a statement on affordability, with 62% approving the referendum. The measure raises the homestead exemption to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, which will mean savings on property tax bills.Local governments that depend on property tax revenue now face tightening budgets by making cuts, reducing services and possibly finding new ways to raise revenue."We don't charge yet for parking downtown, and every time we talk about it, everybody flips out because they don't want it and neither do I," Resch said. "I don't know where we're going to go. I don't know what we're going to do."

Investigators have recovered a portion of an engine from the Learjet 60 that crashed near Greenacres on Sunday as crews continue excavating the crash site, according to the National Transportation Safety Board.The NTSB said excavation work began late Wednesday and continued Thursday as investigators and local officials worked to recover wreckage from the crash that killed nine people.WATCH REPORT BELOW: Part of jet's engine found, NTSB saysDebris from the aircraft has been found away from the main impact site, including on the roofs of nearby homes and buildings, according to the NTSB. A Martin County judge has denied a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, whose trial has been delayed at least nine times since her arrest more than two years ago.Prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed to WPTV that Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense's second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. hearing held Wednesday.Camerlengo's attorneys filed the motion, seeking to have the charges thrown out. Prosecutors opposed the request, filing a motion arguing the defense's amended motion was "procedurally invalid and facially insufficient."Wednesday's ruling means the case against Camerlengo will continue, though a trial date has yet to be set.Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care.Her arrest followed a WPTV investigation that linked at least seven dog deaths or serious injuries to her training and boarding facility over the course of a decade.The latest ruling comes after more than two years of courtroom delays, disputes over expert witnesses and growing frustration from the judge overseeing the case.During a contentious July hearing, Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo's defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial."I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do," Metzger said. "This case has been continued so many times, I've lost count."In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027.That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial.Camerlengo's defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths."I think the detective jumped the gun, so to speak. I don't think she had all of the facts," Kaplan previously told WPTV.Among those closely following the case is Adele Kirk Csontos, whose dog, Mako, died after spending approximately 48 hours at Pawsitively Paradise in November 2022.Kirk Csontos filed a police report following Mako's death, but Camerlengo was never charged in connection with it because his necropsy was inconclusive.Necropsies of two other dogs determined they died from blunt force trauma, leading to Camerlengo's arrest."I mean, I know the wheels of justice turn very slowly, but no, I didn't think it would be two years," Kirk Csontos previously told WPTV.Despite the repeated delays, she said she remains hopeful."I'm still hopeful. Believe it or not, I'm still hopeful that she will be held accountable," she said.Camerlengo's next court appearance, a docket sounding, is scheduled for Dec. 1.No trial date has been announced.

Days after heavy rain moved through the area, floodwaters are still creating problems for local farms and nurseries, forcing some to close to visitors and adding to months of weather-related challenges.WPTV reporter Christy Waite visited Happy Place Ranch in Palm City, where standing water surrounds much of the property as the owners work to recover from the flooding.WATCH REPORT BELOW: For owner Amanda Cimorelli, seeing the ranch underwater has been emotional."It's crushing," Cimorelli said as she fought back tears. The challenge is finding enough dry space for them."I have nowhere to put farm animals. "Just wait and figure it out day by day."Meanwhile, in Loxahatchee Groves, Gardino Nursery is also dealing with flooding after an already difficult year of weather extremes.Owner Sid Gardino said the nursery has endured a freeze, drought and now excess water."The freeze was probably the worst we have experienced," Gardino said. "Then the drought came, and I prayed for rain. I think I prayed too hard because now we have all of this."Water reached shin level in some areas, while thick mud made it difficult to walk around the property."It's frustrating. It's hard to walk with this much rain. We are working at 20% capacity," Gardino said.Gardino Nursery operates by appointment only. The nursery said it is still able to ship products, but customers currently cannot visit the property to see plants in person.The business does not yet know how much revenue has been lost because of the flooding.There is some encouraging news. Gardino said the property is already beginning to recover. They hope that if the sunny and warm weather continues, they can be back open by next week.

Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Palm Beach is balancing four community efforts this week, from responding to people displaced by a plane crash and flooding to opening an interactive museum designed to help people better understand poverty.Ellen T. Wayne, CEO of Catholic Charities of the Diocese of Palm Beach, said the organization has been working with people affected by two emergencies while preparing to welcome the public to the People of Hope Mobile Museum and its “Spare Change, Share Hope” campaign.WATCH REPORT BELOW: “We got hit with a double whammy,” Wayne said. “First, we're responding to the individuals who have been displaced as a result of the plane crash here in Palm Beach County, and then, now we're in full disaster response mode working with individuals who've been impacted by this [recent] flooding that we've had across our five counties in our diocese.”The first two efforts involve Catholic Charities' response to immediate needs in the community.Wayne said the organization has been assisting people displaced by the Palm Beach County plane crash.At the same time, Catholic Charities has moved into disaster response following flooding across the five-county area served by the Diocese of Palm Beach (Okeechobee, Indian River, Martin, St. Lucie and Palm Beach counties).Those efforts are an extension of the organization's everyday work with people experiencing vulnerable situations, Wayne said.The third effort brings a different kind of assistance to the community: understanding.The People of Hope Mobile Museum is a traveling interactive museum housed inside an expandable semi-truck. It is visiting Catholic Charities agencies across the United States and is making a stop at the Cathedral of St. Ignatius Loyola in Palm Beach Gardens.Wayne said the experience is intended to give visitors a glimpse into the lives of people dealing with poverty while sharing stories of resilience, perseverance, and hope.Visitors can experience an interactive simulator that explores situations faced by people living in poverty, record their own stories, and leave messages of hope for others.The museum also explores circumstances faced by seniors, people experiencing homelessness, and other people Catholic Charities serves.“Oftentimes, people, when they're hearing a story of an individual struggling, will think, ‘Well, why did they do that or why didn't they do something else?’” Wayne said. “This is really going to give our guests an opportunity to see the challenges and the decisions that people have to make every day and the reality that there's no easy way out.”The pop-up museum is free to attend Friday and Saturday.The fourth effort happening this weekend is the "Spare Change. Share Hope." campaign.Visitors who want to support Catholic Charities can contribute through a QR code associated with the campaign.The campaign complements the museum's larger message by giving visitors an opportunity to move from learning about challenges their neighbors face to helping people in need.Wayne described that connection by saying Catholic Charities has “people out in the field doing the work of Hope,” while the museum gives others an opportunity to learn what it means to become a person of hope themselves.The timing gives the People of Hope Museum added relevance in Palm Beach County.While Catholic Charities responds to people affected by emergencies, the museum asks visitors to consider the difficult decisions people can face when circumstances suddenly change.“It's always easier to be on the outside looking in,” Wayne said. “This is intended to kind of open our eyes to what the struggles of people who are impoverished all across our country are facing.”The People of Hope Mobile Museum is at the Cathedral of St. Military Trail in Palm Beach Gardens.It is open Friday from 8:30 a.m. and Saturday from 8:30 a.m. Admission is free.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Palm Beach County students are helping scientists answer a deceptively simple question: Where does our trash go once it starts floating through local waterways?ANGARI Foundation plans to release bright orange, eco-friendly drift cards into the water on Nov. 10 at noon as part of its Lagoon Drift Card Study. Members of the public are then being asked to find the cards and report where they ended up.“So we're basically trying to track our trash,” Laura Jessop with ANGARI Foundation told WPTV. “So we put these eco-friendly drift cards in the water. They're going in on November 10 at 12 p.m., and we need the public to go out and find them.”The idea is to use the cards as stand-ins for other objects floating on the surface.“Everything that floats on the surface, that's what we're sort of tracking right now,” Jessop said.Each card found by a member of the public becomes another piece of information for the study.Jessop said knowing where the cards eventually turn up can help researchers identify places where floating debris could be accumulating.“They're bright orange, and if they report them to us, we can then look at where our trash is accumulating and really target those areas,” she said.The project involves Manatee Lagoon, where some of the drift cards will be released.Rachel Shanker with Manatee Lagoon said participating in the project can provide information that may ultimately help protect Florida's environment.“Here at Manatee Lagoon, we're so excited to be a part of this study where we can collect data and learn how to better preserve and protect Florida's environment and wildlife for future generations,” Shanker said.The study isn't limited to scientists and environmental organizations.Students from Palm Springs Community Middle School are creating their own drift cards and will release them at Manatee Lagoon on Nov. 10.A teacher participating in the project told WPTV the experiment gives students the opportunity to connect what they're studying in class with an actual environmental project.“My students are creating drift cards which they will be releasing on November 10 here at Manatee Lagoon, and they are doing this to track the pollution in the waterways and apply what we're learning in the classroom to the real world,” she said.And the students aren't sending anonymous pieces of orange material into the water.They're making the cards their own.One student decorated a card with water, a sun and a shark, before adding a marine-themed message: “You're 'fintastic.'”Another decorated a card as an ocean scene with a simple message for whoever eventually discovers it: “Love your ocean.”For students, the cards turn an environmental lesson into something tangible.They create the cards, release them, and wait to see where currents carry them. If members of the public find and report their locations, those discoveries become part of the study.That provides a real-world demonstration of something that can otherwise be difficult to visualize in a classroom: What happens to floating material after it enters a waterway?For the broader community, it also turns a walk along the water into an opportunity to participate in local science.If you spot one of the bright orange drift cards, it may be more than something that washed ashore. Its location is precisely the information researchers are looking for.The experiment comes just before another important date for the Lake Worth Lagoon.Manatee season officially begins Nov. 15.Shanker said cooler temperatures help bring manatees back toward Manatee Lagoon.“As the water temperatures drop, they start coming here to Manatee Lagoon for our warm water outflow,” Shanker said.Manatee Lagoon plans to celebrate the beginning of the season with a kickoff event Nov. 21.For the students creating drift cards, meanwhile, the next milestone comes Nov. 10, when their colorful creations leave their hands and begin their journey through South Florida's waterways.Where they end up is part of the experiment.Who finds them could be anyone.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Five days after historic rainfall flooded parts of the Treasure Coast, residents along Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach are still dealing with several feet of standing water inside their homes, with little indication of when it will recede. The street remains accessible only by boat or kayak, with floodwaters reaching mailboxes and entering most homes along the road. For longtime resident Linda Weisbecker, the flooding has left decades of memories and belongings underwater. “Sixty years of your life is gone. We raised our kids, our grandkids, our great-grandkids. It’s all gone,” Weisbecker said. Weisbecker said her home still has several feet of water inside, preventing her from beginning the cleanup process. “Our main goal is to get this water off so we can get in and start getting things done. If we don’t, it’s going to be that much worse,” she said. Just down the road, Lisa French is dealing with similar conditions. French said her home initially avoided flooding during Monday’s heavy rainfall. However, as water continued to accumulate in the neighborhood, it eventually entered her home two days later. Now, she is concerned about mold growth and how much of her home may need to be torn out and replaced. We’re a single-family income. I stay at home with my kids. So it’s, you know, we don’t even know where to start. And we can’t start because the water is still here,” French said. The affected neighborhood sits near the Savannas Preserve, an area where water can naturally flow south when surrounding land becomes oversaturated. Martin County officials told WPBF 25 News that crews will be working to address flooding concerns and evaluate local watersheds to determine whether they have sufficient capacity to handle floodwaters. Floodwater has covered much of the pasture at a Martin County farm, leaving its Florida Cracker cattle crowded onto a narrow strip of higher ground as flooding continues in the Trailside community. At Hungryland Farms , the cattle’s usual grazing areas are underwater. The herd has been moved onto the farm’s elevated driveway and house pad, owner Melissa Chirico told CBS12 News. The farm is concerned about the animals’ safety and how long they may have to remain there. The flooding has also affected other ranches and properties in the neighborhood, according to residents and Trailside homeowners association leaders. They say water continued rising even after the rain stopped and have raised concerns about a drainage breach near county-owned land. Martin County acquired a 315-acre parcel known as the Elise J. property in March 2026 for conservation purposes. The county has said it is working with the Hobe-St. Lucie Conservancy District on a breach affecting drainage into an irrigation canal. The agencies determined repairs should wait until water levels recede, the county said, citing safety concerns and the risk of damaging the levee. The county is also evaluating longer-term options to improve outflow and reduce future flood risk. The county has said its immediate priority is establishing access to assess conditions. It plans to make repairs when crews can work safely without compromising the levee. See also: Water in the gas: Pumps shut off, driver reports costly repairs after South Florida floods The cattle at Hungryland Farms are Florida Cracker cattle , a rare heritage breed recognized by Florida as the state’s official heritage cattle breed. Descended from cattle brought to Florida by the Spanish in the 1500s, the breed is valued for its connection to the state’s agricultural history. The farm’s photographs and those taken by CBS12's Christopher Pollock show cattle standing on dry ground beside broad areas of standing water. Melissa said the flooding has cut off much of the property and left the herd with limited dry space. The drainage system and the source and volume of water flowing into the area remain central questions for residents.

Law enforcement officials in St. Lucie County announced Thursday that 40 suspected members of a Fort Pierce gang have been arrested following an 18-month investigation. The investigation, known as "Operation Score Board," targeted the 23rd Street Gang, which authorities say has operated in northern St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said the gang has between 70 and 80 members and has been responsible for years of violence in the Fort Pierce community. "This gang has terrorized, basically created a hostage crisis for our community up there," Del Toro said. "There’s a lot of good people that are up there in Fort Pierce that have been just held hostage by this group for the last decade, living in fear." Investigators said the gang even maintained a scoreboard tracking shootings and homicides, a discovery that ultimately gave the operation its name. Fort Pierce Police Chief David Smith said detectives reviewed a decade of criminal activity to identify connections between suspected gang members and violent crimes. "Detectives conducted an extensive review of criminal activity spanning ten years, examining incidents and identifying connections between individuals associated with the gang," Smith said. "This intensive analysis revealed a disturbing pattern of organized crime and violence." Authorities said investigators used Florida’s RICO law to connect years of alleged shootings, drug trafficking and other criminal activity to members of the 23rd Street Gang. The investigation involved multiple local and state law enforcement agencies working together over 18 months to build cases against suspected members of the organization. On Wednesday, law enforcement officers executed multiple search warrants throughout the Fort Pierce area, resulting in 11 arrests as part of the larger operation. Authorities said officers also seized multiple firearms, drugs and thousands of dollars in cash. Del Toro said the size of the operation and the cooperation between agencies could have a lasting impact on the community. "I’ve never seen an operation this large with this many agencies at the local and federal level," Del Toro said. "I think this is going to have a significant generational impact in this community." Authorities said similar investigations and operations are expected in the future.
