hero.headline: Indian River County public schools to remain closed Friday, plan Monday reopening
hero.body:
Indian River County public schools will stay closed Friday, Nov. 6, because flooding is still interfering with transportation and access to some campuses. The district plans to welcome students back Monday, Nov. 9. Officials cited a shortage of available bus drivers and major delays on County Roads 510 and 512 as reasons for keeping schools closed Friday. School buildings will be open to instructional staff so they can prepare for the planned return Monday. The reopening remains a plan as the district continues to watch conditions and provide updates through its official communication channels.

St. Lucie County public schools also will remain closed Friday, with classes expected to resume Monday. Flooding has made some roads and bus stops inaccessible and has complicated access to some school campuses. The problems extend beyond school property: Some families and district employees still have no electricity, while others cannot safely get out of their neighborhoods. Those ongoing transportation and access issues are affecting the district’s return to school. St. Lucie officials said they will continue monitoring conditions and issuing updates through official channels. The district also will provide information about any required instructional make-up days when that information becomes available.

The St. Lucie district canceled athletic activities through Sunday, with athletics potentially returning Monday. The SAT that had been scheduled for Saturday, Nov. 7, has been rescheduled. The planned Monday return for both school districts follows continued flooding that has disrupted travel to schools and left some families unable to leave home safely. In Indian River County, the district’s Friday arrangements allow instructional staff into buildings to prepare even though schools remain closed to students. In St. Lucie County, the district’s announcement also addresses the disruption to athletics and the weekend SAT, in addition to Friday’s school closure.

Five Boys & Girls Clubs locations in St. Lucie County will open at 8 a.m. for current members and children interested in joining. Each site can serve up to 100 members, and members may attend any location. Families can register at bgcofslc.org. Children should bring their own packed lunch, a snack and a water bottle. Locations include Chuck Hill at 198 Marion Ave.; Ken Pruitt at 10673 SE Lennard Road in Port St. Lucie; Percy Peek Teen at 2902 Avenue D in Fort Pierce; and Garden Terrace at 3104 Avenue J in Fort Pierce. The clubs’ announcement gives families a separate option while public schools remain closed.

hero.headline: About 75% of Creekside homes evacuated as flooding keeps power off in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Roughly 75% of homes in St. Lucie County’s Creekside community have been evacuated, and electricity remains shut off amid flooding, St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Thursday. Some Florida Power & Light equipment remains underwater, and crews must wait for water to recede enough to safely restore power.

The neighborhood, off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike, has about 150 homes and remains under a voluntary evacuation. Floodwaters are still knee-deep in parts of the community. Del Toro said some trucks can now enter the neighborhood, though water levels remain high.

Deputies are providing 24-hour security while residents remain displaced and electricity is out. A high-water vehicle is also available to help residents who need assistance. Del Toro urged residents to contact deputies or call 911 if they need help.

“We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else,” Florida Power & Light's Marshall Critchfield said. “Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety.”

Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as the water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. Del Toro said Creekside has underground utilities, creating an additional challenge while floodwaters remain high.

cards.teaser: A 12-inch pump began moving an estimated 7,000 to 8,000 gallons of floodwater per minute Wednesday night. Routine evacuations were suspended overnight, while responders remained available for fire and medical emergencies.
cards.body:
A high-capacity pump began moving floodwater out of the Vitalia community in Port St. Lucie on Wednesday night, and routine evacuations were suspended overnight, according to the St. Lucie County Fire District. Evacuations were scheduled to resume at 6:30 a.m. Thursday, while emergency responders remained available for fire and medical emergencies.

The City of Port St. Lucie Public Works Department installed the 12-inch pump, which began operating at approximately 8 p.m. Wednesday, the fire district said. It was moving an estimated 7,000 to 8,000 gallons of water per minute to help reduce flooding in the neighborhood. The overnight suspension applied to routine evacuation operations. Residents with immediate safety concerns or serious medical concerns requiring assistance were instructed to call 911.

By Wednesday evening, the St. Lucie County Fire District had responded to 135 high-water rescue incidents countywide. The flooding had continued for more than 48 hours. Although the heaviest rain had moved through, police warned that water could take days to recede and that conditions could change quickly.

Among those evacuated Wednesday were Vitalia residents Sheri George and her husband, Arthur. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission brought them out on a swamp buggy after flooded roads prevented them from driving out of the neighborhood. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me,” Guogas said.

cards.teaser: The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School to help public schools reopen. The county is also relocating its special medical needs shelter.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management plans to move its general population flood shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. The relocation was scheduled for Wednesday morning, along with a move for the special medical needs shelter currently at the Fenn Center.

On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts.

Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where water can drain. Officials urge residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads, stay out of closed roadways and never go around barricades. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: About 75% of Creekside homes evacuated in St. Lucie County; power remains off
hero.body:
Roughly 75% of homes in the flooded Creekside community in St. Lucie County have been evacuated, and power remains shut off, Sheriff Richard Del Toro said Thursday. Floodwaters remain knee-deep in parts of the neighborhood, and submerged Florida Power & Light equipment must become safely accessible before crews can restore electricity.

The community has about 150 homes off State Road 70 west of Florida's Turnpike and remains under a voluntary evacuation, Del Toro said. Some trucks can now enter the neighborhood, but water levels remain high. The neighborhood has underground utilities, which Del Toro said creates an additional challenge while flooding persists.

FPL's Marshall Critchfield said crews will restore electricity as soon as the water recedes enough for them to safely access the equipment. “We continue to monitor the water level just like everybody else,” Critchfield said. “Much of our equipment is presently underwater and our priority number one, as always, is safety.”

Deputies are providing 24-hour security in Creekside while residents remain displaced and electricity is out, Del Toro said. The sheriff's office also has a high-water vehicle available to assist residents who need help. “If in fact you need help, please don't hesitate to call 911 or contact one of our deputies,” Del Toro said.

hero.headline: Vitalia evacuations paused overnight as Port St. Lucie starts floodwater pump
hero.body:
Routine evacuations in Port St. Lucie’s flooded Vitalia community were suspended overnight as a newly installed pump began moving water out of the neighborhood Wednesday evening, the St. Lucie County Fire District said. Evacuations were scheduled to resume at 6:30 a.m. Thursday. Emergency responders remain available for fire and medical emergencies, and residents with immediate safety concerns or serious medical needs requiring assistance should call 911.

The City of Port St. Lucie Public Works Department installed the 12-inch pump, which began operating at approximately 8 p.m. Wednesday to help reduce flooding in Vitalia, according to the fire district. Flooding had continued for more than 48 hours. Although the heaviest rain had moved through, police warned that water could take days to recede and conditions could change quickly. As of Wednesday evening, the fire district had responded to 135 high-water rescue incidents countywide. Police urged residents to follow evacuation instructions, stay out of floodwaters and avoid closed or barricaded roads.

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission evacuated Vitalia resident Sheri George and her husband Arthur on a swamp buggy Wednesday. Flooded roads had prevented them from driving out of the neighborhood, and food in their refrigerator was spoiling during a power outage. “This is definitely, whoever's idea this was, thank you. 'Cause otherwise we would've been stuck there, who knows how much longer,” Sheri George said. Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident evacuated because of flooding, questioned the community’s preparedness. “I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me,” Guogas said.

FWC said it had evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater since Tuesday. Jon Arnold, an FWC investigator, was driving a swamp buggy at Vitalia. “I'm glad all the communities here pulled together, all the first responders, law enforcement. We had a plan together and made it happen, and we were able to get a lot of people out to safety,” said Tyson Matthews, FWC Public Information Officer.

cards.teaser: The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School to help public schools reopen. The special medical needs shelter is also relocating from the Fenn Center.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management planned to move its general population flood shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce on Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. The special medical needs shelter, housed at the Fenn Center, was also set to relocate.

On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several Port St. Lucie locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts.

Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where water can drain. Officials urge residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and services affected by flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

Monday’s heavy rain saturated the ground and overwhelmed the drainage system. Martin County said it was unable to pump water out of the neighborhood because the nearby watershed lacked capacity.

At French’s home, water had reached 4 inches deep and was continuing to climb. Her husband made a mark inside to track the rising level. “My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else,” French said.

Both residents were confronting damage to their homes while the flooding continued. “Even after, like, our houses are wrecked,” French said. Kincaid described the strain: “It's just a lot to take in right now for us.”

St. Lucie County Emergency Management was moving its general population flood shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce on Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. The special medical needs shelter also was being relocated from the Fenn Center.

On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Recovery efforts continued across Port St. Lucie as water levels receded in some areas. Significant standing water remained at SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard.

Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continued checking on residents, monitoring roadways and helping people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations also were supporting recovery efforts and working to restore normal conditions safely.

Officials warned that water levels could take several days to recede. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain.

Residents are urged to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. Officials also encouraged people to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by the flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: Vitalia routine evacuations paused overnight as pump starts in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
Routine evacuations in Port St. Lucie’s flooded Vitalia community were suspended overnight and were scheduled to resume at 6:30 a.m. Thursday, according to the St. Lucie County Fire District. A newly installed pump began operating Wednesday evening as dangerous flooding continued to affect neighborhoods more than 48 hours into the emergency. Fire and medical emergency response remained available during the pause in routine evacuations. The fire district directed residents with immediate safety concerns or serious medical needs requiring assistance to call 911.

The City of Port St. Lucie Public Works Department installed the 12-inch pump in Vitalia, where it began operating at approximately 8 p.m. Wednesday, the fire district said. The pump was moving an estimated 7,000 to 8,000 gallons of water per minute to help reduce neighborhood flooding. As of Wednesday evening, the fire district had responded to 135 high-water rescue incidents across St. Lucie County. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said it had evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater since Tuesday. Police warned that water could take days to recede and that conditions could change quickly, even after the heaviest rain had moved through.

Vitalia resident Sheri George and her husband Arthur were evacuated Wednesday aboard a Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission swamp buggy. Flooded roads had prevented them from driving out of the neighborhood, and food in their refrigerator was spoiling. Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident evacuated because of flooding, questioned the preparation for the emergency. “I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me,” Guogas said.

Flooding also affected Valencia Cay at Riverland, where some residents were unable to get their cars out of their driveways because streets were flooded. Some residents said water reached their garages. Street flooding reached 18 inches deep. Police urged residents to follow evacuation instructions, stay out of floodwaters and avoid closed or barricaded roads. They also encouraged residents to check on neighbors and vulnerable loved ones when they could do so safely.

cards.headline: St. Lucie Public Schools remain closed Thursday amid flooded roads and bus stops
cards.teaser: Schools are expected to reopen Friday, Nov. 6, but the district said that could change depending on conditions.
cards.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools will remain closed Thursday, Nov. 5, because of flooded roads and bus stops following this week's severe weather. The district announced the continued closure Wednesday as high water remained in parts of the county.

District officials said they want to allow additional time for flooding to subside before returning to normal operations. Essential employees are required to report to work as outlined in the district's Emergency Operations Plan.

Schools are expected to reopen Friday, Nov. 6, but the district cautioned that the reopening could change depending on conditions. Families are encouraged to check the St. Lucie Public Schools website for updates before schools reopen.

cards.headline: Water rises in Hyline Drive homes in Jensen Beach as full watershed blocks pumping
cards.teaser: Water was still rising inside some homes Wednesday afternoon after Monday's heavy rain overwhelmed drainage. Martin County said the nearby watershed was too full to receive water pumped from the neighborhood.
cards.body:
Water was still rising inside some homes on Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon, long after the rain stopped. Martin County said it could not pump water out of the flooded neighborhood because the nearby watershed lacked capacity to receive it.

Dozens of homes were underwater after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and overwhelmed the drainage system. The neighborhood sits next to the Savannas Preserve, where water from other flooded areas is naturally flowing south, according to the county.

Residents Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid have been using a kayak to get around their flooded community. Water at Kincaid's home was waist-deep. “We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can,” Kincaid said.

At French's home, water had reached 4 inches deep and was continuing to rise. French said her husband had marked the water level inside to track its climb. “My floorboards are outside, but it's still rising. My husband made a mark inside so it's still coming up and ours isn't nearly as bad as everyone else,” she said.

Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said lower water levels would allow the county to pump into nearby ponds. “As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,” Gordon said. “We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.”

cards.headline: St. Lucie County reports 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls
cards.body:
St. Lucie County emergency crews had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls amid widespread flooding, officials said Tuesday. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday, Nov. 4. Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel, saying water could take several days to recede. Public Safety Director Ron Guerrero said estimated rainfall totals reached 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Flooding affected Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards, as well as Virginia Avenue.

The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. The county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Crews continued high-water rescues, assessed roads and infrastructure, and worked to clear drainage and roadways. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns.

Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised avoiding standing water, especially with cuts or open wounds, and washing with soap and water after exposure. Residents should not eat food or use household items that touched floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water, boil tap water or disinfect it. Flood-affected private wells should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

The school district hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions, and planned to assess whether roads were passable before reopening. Officials warned that road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000. The city also warned of a one-day solid waste collection delay, with collection shifting to the next service day, including Saturday.

The county’s public safety director, Ron Guerrero, said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Officials said the flooding affected areas across the county, including Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards and Virginia Avenue. He advised residents to avoid contact with standing water, especially if they have cuts or open wounds, and to wash with soap and water if exposed. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that came into contact with floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Sperber said health officials planned to assess mobile home parks for flood-related health and safety concerns. Residents with questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can call 772-873-4931 . Private wells affected by flooding should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

hero.headline: Evacuations continue in Port St. Lucie's Vitalia as floodwaters could linger for days
hero.body:
Police are evacuating residents from the flooded Vitalia community in Port St. Lucie as dangerous water persists more than 48 hours into the flooding emergency. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission said it has evacuated about 300 people trapped by floodwater across several affected areas since Tuesday. Police warned that water could take days to recede and conditions could change quickly.

FWC evacuated Vitalia resident Sheri George and her husband, Arthur, aboard a swamp buggy Wednesday. Flooded roads had prevented them from driving out of the neighborhood. They had no electricity or air conditioning, and food in their refrigerator was spoiling. George said she was thankful for the evacuation, which got the couple safely out of the community. Andrea Guogas, another Vitalia resident, also was evacuated because of flooding. “I don't understand why it happened. I just, I don't understand why we're not better prepared for something like this living in Florida, quite frankly. This is crazy to me,” Guogas said.

FWC investigator Jon Arnold was driving a swamp buggy at Vitalia as crews helped residents leave. FWC Public Information Officer Tyson Matthews credited cooperation among communities, first responders and law enforcement. “I'm glad all the communities here pulled together, all the first responders, law enforcement. We had a plan together and made it happen, and we were able to get a lot of people out to safety,” Matthews said.

In Valencia Cay at Riverland, some residents said flooded streets left them effectively trapped at home and unable to get their cars out of their driveways. Some said water had reached their garages but had not entered their homes. Although the heaviest rain has moved through, police said officers and emergency personnel continued helping residents get to safety. Police urged residents to follow evacuation instructions, never drive or walk through floodwaters, avoid closed or barricaded roads, and check on neighbors and vulnerable loved ones when they can do so safely.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie offers up to $25,000 for flood repairs through $1 million program
cards.teaser: Eligible homeowners can receive forgivable loans for emergency repairs after this week’s flooding. Mold remediation is excluded and must be completed before approved repairs can proceed.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie has allocated $1 million to help income-eligible homeowners repair damage from this week’s flooding, offering up to $25,000 per eligible homeowner through its Disaster Relief Program. The assistance comes as 0% interest deferred-payment loans with no monthly payments, forgiven over five years under program guidelines.

The program serves low- and moderate-income homeowners making emergency repairs to their primary residences within city limits. Applicants must meet income guidelines, have owned and occupied their homes for at least one year, and have an assessed home value of $560,154 or less. They must also be current on mortgage and property tax payments. Funded by the Florida Housing Finance Corporation as part of the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP), the program will continue until its funding is exhausted.

Mold and mildew inspection, testing, removal and remediation are excluded from funding. Homeowners must complete any necessary mold remediation before approved repairs can proceed, though eligible repairs may be funded once remediation is complete. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or non-permitted work are also ineligible for assistance.

Covered expenses include tree and debris removal needed to restore habitability, homeowner insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further property damage. Repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, and temporary structural stabilization. All work must be directly related to the declared disaster, necessary to preserve the property’s safety and integrity, and approved by the city before assistance is provided.

Residents may complete the program’s pre-application online. For assistance, homeowners can contact the city’s Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, email Housing@cityofpsl.com or visit City Hall.

cards.teaser: The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School as St. Lucie County relocates two shelters to help public schools reopen. Twenty-one people were staying at the shelters Wednesday.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its general population flood shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce on Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen. The county is also relocating its special medical needs shelter from the Fenn Center as residents displaced by this week’s flooding continue to need accommodation.

On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help displaced residents.

Flooding continues in parts of St. Lucie County. Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts.

Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain.

Officials are urging residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by the flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: Water rises in Jensen Beach homes on Hyline Drive as Martin County cannot pump it out
hero.body:
Water was still rising inside some homes on Hyline Drive in Jensen Beach on Wednesday afternoon, long after the rain stopped. Martin County said it cannot pump water out of the flooded neighborhood because the nearby watershed remains at capacity.

Dozens of homes are underwater after Monday's heavy rain saturated the ground and overwhelmed the drainage system. The neighborhood sits next to the Savannas Preserve, where water from other flooded areas is naturally flowing south, according to the county.

Residents Lisa French and Tiffany Kincaid have been using a kayak to get around their flooded community. At Kincaid's home, the water is waist-deep. “We're currently taking stuff out of our house right now, salvaging what we can,” Kincaid said.

At French's home, water had reached 4 inches deep and was continuing to climb. French said her husband marked the water level inside to track its rise. Her floorboards were outside, and she said other homes were in worse condition.

Martin County's Public Works Director Jim Gordon said lower water levels would allow the ponds that receive pumped water to drain, creating room for the county to begin pumping out the neighborhood.

“As the water level drops, that's going to drain the ponds that we need to pump into, and that's going to allow us to do that,” Gordon said. “We're maximizing what we can downstream, and we might see it trending in the right direction.”

Residents are trying to salvage belongings while facing damage to their homes. “It's just a lot to take in right now for us,” Kincaid said.

The district announced the extended closure Wednesday, saying it wants to allow more time for flooding to subside before returning to normal operations.

Schools are expected to reopen Friday, Nov. 6, but the district cautioned that reopening could change depending on conditions. Families are encouraged to check the St. Lucie Public Schools website for updates before schools reopen. Essential employees must report to work as outlined in the district's Emergency Operations Plan.

“Thank you for your patience and understanding as our community recovers from this unprecedented weather event,” the district said.

cards.headline: Steven Giordano defeats Shannon Martin in Port St. Lucie mayoral race
cards.teaser: Giordano won by just over 2,400 votes, reversing an August primary result in which Martin finished nearly 13 percentage points ahead of him.
cards.body:
Steven Giordano defeated incumbent Shannon Martin for Port St. Lucie mayor by just over 2,400 votes, reversing their standings in the August primary. Martin had finished nearly 13 percentage points ahead of Giordano in that contest.

Giordano celebrated with supporters Tuesday night at Recovery Sports Grill in Tradition after pulling ahead with more than 51% of the vote. At his election-night watch party, he said he believed voters responded to his message and approach to the race. "I think they saw somebody that was dedicated, that was here for all the right reasons," Giordano said. "I think they watched the debate."

Giordano said he wants to serve residents rather than approach the position as a politician. "I think they saw somebody who is here for all the right reasons, that's not a politician, that's not here for money, that's here to do the right thing for the people," he said. "And I'm proud to be the people's mayor."

The general election followed a contentious August primary that included an FDLE investigation involving campaign signs. The investigation led to Martin's husband and two other Port St. Lucie police officers being placed on paid administrative leave.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County moving flood shelter to Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: The general population shelter is relocating from Northport K-8 School to help public schools reopen. Sixteen people were staying at the shelter Wednesday.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its general population flood shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce on Wednesday to help St. Lucie Public Schools reopen. The relocation comes as flooding continues in parts of the county and recovery crews work to restore normal conditions.

Sixteen people were staying at the general population shelter Wednesday, while five were at the special medical needs shelter. The special medical needs shelter is also relocating from the Fenn Center. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations in Port St. Lucie, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain.

Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts. Officials urge residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

cards.headline: Family questions walking safety on Port St. Lucie Boulevard after teen's death
cards.teaser: Jacory Brown's family is raising concerns about construction and walking conditions after the Treasure Coast High School freshman was killed Oct. 7. A road-widening project is expected to finish in winter 2028.
cards.body:
The family of Jacory Brown, a Treasure Coast High School freshman killed while walking to school Oct. 7, is raising concerns about walking conditions along Port St. Lucie Boulevard. His family says construction makes the road dangerous for children traveling to school on foot.

Brown was struck and killed by a car early that morning. His mother, Shelly-Ann Findley-Brown, described puddles and inadequate sidewalks along the road, saying rain the night before had left water in the area.

“The road conditions are horrible,” Findley-Brown said. “You are walking in puddles. And the night before, it rained. There was water all over the place.”

FDOT began construction in 2025 to widen the road from two lanes to four. The project, which includes adding sidewalks and lights, is expected to be completed in winter 2028.

“I hope the state takes this into a big consideration because it's not right walking to school when you don't have proper sidewalks,” Findley-Brown said.

Jacory's parents, Findley-Brown and Ainsworth Brown, and his grandfather, Clovis Brown, are remembering his smile and friendliness. Jacory also had a passion for entrepreneurship and graphic design, creating cover art, business cards and flyers for friends and family.

“He just went to school,” Findley-Brown said. “He was supposed to come back home. His birthday would be on Monday. He would have been 15.”

Jacory will be laid to rest Nov. 14. Friends have started a GoFundMe to support the family.

hero.headline: Martin County judge rejects dismissal of Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo’s cruelty case
hero.body:
A Martin County judge on Wednesday rejected a motion to dismiss the felony animal cruelty case against Palm City dog trainer Nikki Camerlengo, allowing the prosecution to continue after at least nine trial delays since her arrest more than two years ago.

Judge Elizabeth Metzger denied the defense’s second amended motion to dismiss during a 9 a.m. hearing, prosecutor Kristen Chase confirmed. Prosecutors had opposed the request to throw out the charges, arguing in a court filing that the defense’s amended motion was “procedurally invalid and facially insufficient.”

Camerlengo, the owner of Pawsitively Paradise in Palm City, was arrested in June 2024 on two felony animal cruelty charges after Martin County detectives said two dogs died while in her care. Necropsies determined that the two dogs died from blunt force trauma, leading to her arrest.

The case has faced repeated delays and disputes over expert witnesses. At a contentious hearing in July, Metzger questioned both prosecutors and Camerlengo’s defense team about why the case had yet to go to trial.

“I wanted you here, because I thought I was very clear in the past on what you needed to do,” Metzger said. “This case has been continued so many times, I've lost count.”

In September, the trial was delayed for a ninth time after prosecutors told the court that a key witness was on medical disability and would be unable to testify until at least the end of January 2027. That witness must first testify at a hearing to determine whether she will be permitted to testify at trial.

Camerlengo’s defense attorney, Stuart Kaplan, has also sought to exclude testimony from the Texas veterinary pathologist who performed necropsies on the two dogs and the lead detective who investigated their deaths.

Camerlengo’s next court appearance, a docket sounding, is scheduled for Dec. 1.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie to open applications Thursday for $1 million in flood-repair aid
cards.teaser: Eligible homeowners can receive up to $25,000 through loans forgiven over five years. Pre-applications open at 8 a.m. Thursday.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie will open pre-applications at 8 a.m. Thursday for its $1 million Disaster Relief Program, which helps low- and moderate-income homeowners repair primary residences damaged by this week's flooding. The city announced the allocation Wednesday. Eligible homeowners can receive up to $25,000, and the program will remain open until the funding is exhausted.

The assistance comes through the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program, with funding from the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. It is offered as a 0% interest deferred-payment loan with no monthly payments. The loans are forgiven over five years in accordance with program guidelines. Applicants must meet the program's income requirements and must have owned and occupied their home within Port St. Lucie city limits for at least one year. The home's assessed value must be $560,154 or less, and applicants must be current on mortgage and property tax payments.

According to the city, the money can pay for emergency repairs and other work needed to make a flood-damaged home safe and habitable. Eligible expenses may include tree and debris removal necessary to restore habitability, homeowners insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further damage. Those repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, and temporary structural stabilization. Other reasonable and necessary actions to protect the home from additional damage may also qualify. All work must be directly connected to the declared disaster and approved by the city before assistance is provided.

The program excludes mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal and remediation. Homeowners whose properties require mold remediation must complete that work before other approved repairs can proceed. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or unpermitted work are also excluded.

Residents can apply through the city's housing website. Homeowners who need help can contact Port St. Lucie's Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, email Housing@cityofpsl.com or visit City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Lucie Blvd.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County flood shelter moving to Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce
cards.teaser: The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School as flood recovery continues. Standing water remains at several Port St. Lucie locations, and officials warn drivers to stay off closed roads.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its general population shelter from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce on Wednesday as flood recovery continues. The move is part of a relocation of the county’s general population and special medical needs shelters to help St. Lucie public schools reopen.

On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The special medical needs shelter is relocating from the Fenn Center. The county opened the temporary shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several Port St. Lucie locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain.

Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts. Officials urge drivers to watch for flooded roads, never go around barricades and stay off closed roadways. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by the flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

cards.body:
The sheriff’s office and the Fort Pierce Police Department executed multiple search warrants in St. Lucie County Wednesday morning as part of a criminal investigation. Fort Pierce police officers arrested a woman and placed her in a police car during the operation.

The sheriff’s office warned residents they may see an increased law enforcement presence in some areas as the operation continues. Residents are asked to avoid areas where law enforcement activity is occurring and follow directions from personnel at the scene.

The sheriff’s office said there is no threat to the community.

hero.headline: Live Martin County election results for the 2026 Florida midterm election
hero.body:
Follow live election results for Martin County as voting returns show how contests are taking shape in Florida’s 2026 midterm election. The election coverage brings together Martin County results, statewide races, Florida House contests and proposed constitutional amendments. Readers can follow the county’s returns while also checking the broader Florida midterm election coverage. The results listings provide ways to move between coverage of individual offices and county-level election pages. Martin County is one of four counties included in the regional results listings, alongside Palm Beach, St. Lucie and Indian River counties.

Statewide race coverage includes the contests for Florida governor, attorney general and chief financial officer, as well as the race for a Florida seat in the U.S. Senate. Each office has its own listing within the election coverage, allowing readers to follow a particular contest or return to the overall Florida midterm results. For those watching Martin County, these statewide race listings sit alongside the county results page. Together, they organize coverage by both location and office, with separate entries for the governor’s race, the attorney general’s race, the chief financial officer’s race and the U.S. Senate contest.

The legislative contests listed in the coverage are Florida House Districts 22, 23 and 25. Readers following those races can select the district they want to track, separate from the statewide office listings. The ballot-measure coverage includes three numbered amendments. Amendment 1 concerns the state’s budget stabilization fund. Amendment 2 addresses a personal property tax exemption for agricultural operations. Amendment 3 concerns an increase in the homestead tax exemption. These amendment listings appear with the candidate contests in the election coverage, providing separate places to follow the proposals as well as races for state and federal office.

Regional election listings extend beyond Martin County to results pages for Palm Beach County, St. Lucie County and Indian River County. Other entries in the coverage include the Port St. Lucie mayoral contest, a solid waste pickup referendum and the Palm Beach County clerk’s race. Those listings offer additional paths for readers following elections elsewhere in the region. For Martin County readers, the county results page remains the place to check how the local vote is shaping up, with the broader coverage also providing access to statewide contests, the three listed Florida House races and the three constitutional amendment proposals.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie allocates $1 million for flood repairs; pre-applications open Thursday
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie has allocated $1 million to help eligible homeowners repair damage from this week's flooding, with pre-applications opening at 8 a.m. Thursday. The city's Disaster Relief Program offers up to $25,000 per eligible homeowner for critical repairs to primary residences. Assistance is limited to low- and moderate-income homeowners and will remain available only until the $1 million allocation is exhausted.

The city announced the allocation Wednesday. Assistance is offered through the State Housing Initiatives Partnership (SHIP) program, with funding from the Florida Housing Finance Corporation. Homeowners can receive a 0% interest deferred-payment loan with no monthly payments. The loans are forgiven over five years under program guidelines.

Applicants must meet the program's income requirements and must have owned and occupied their home within Port St. Lucie city limits for at least one year. The home's assessed value must be $560,154 or less. Homeowners also must be current on their mortgage and property tax payments.

The money may cover emergency repairs and other work needed to make a flood-damaged home safe and habitable. Eligible expenses include tree and debris removal needed to restore habitability, payment of homeowners insurance deductibles for eligible rehabilitation work, and temporary repairs to prevent further property damage. Those repairs may include roof repairs, weatherproofing, water extraction, removal of water-damaged materials, emergency plumbing or electrical work, and temporary structural stabilization. Other reasonable and necessary actions to protect the home from additional damage may also qualify. All work must be directly connected to the declared disaster and approved by the city before assistance is provided.

The program excludes mold or mildew inspection, testing, removal and remediation. Homeowners whose properties require mold remediation must complete that work before other approved repairs can proceed. Manufactured homes, pools, hot tubs, and illegal or unpermitted work are also excluded.

Residents can submit pre-applications through the city's housing website beginning Thursday morning. Homeowners seeking help can contact Port St. Lucie's Neighborhood Services Department at 772-344-4084, email Housing@cityofpsl.com or visit City Hall at 121 SW Port St. Lucie Blvd.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Public Schools to remain closed Thursday as bus stops and roads stay flooded
hero.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools will remain closed Thursday, Nov. 5, because numerous bus stops remain flooded and high water continues to affect roads after this week's severe weather. The district announced the continued closure Wednesday, saying it wants to allow more time for flooding to subside before returning to normal operations.

Schools are expected to reopen Friday, Nov. 6, but the district cautioned that the reopening could change depending on conditions. Families are encouraged to check the St. Lucie Public Schools website for updates before schools reopen. Essential employees are required to report to work as outlined in the district's Emergency Operations Plan.

“Thank you for your patience and understanding as our community recovers from this unprecedented weather event,” the district said.

cards.headline: David Jolly wins St. Lucie County as turnout rises despite flooding
cards.teaser: Democrat David Jolly received approximately 51% of the county’s vote for governor. Turnout exceeded the 2022 rate despite flooding that forced polling place relocations.
cards.body:
Democrat David Jolly won St. Lucie County in Tuesday’s governor’s race, carrying approximately 51% of the vote to Republican Byron Donalds’ 48% as turnout rose despite flooding that forced last-minute polling place changes. The result marked the first time since 2012 that a Democratic candidate for governor or president won a majority of the county’s vote. Former President Barack Obama carried St. Lucie County with 53.42% that year. Jolly’s county victory came as election officials moved several voting locations because of flooding across Port St. Lucie, Tradition and Fort Pierce.

Voter turnout reached 56.5%, an increase of 5.2 percentage points from the 2022 general election, when 51.3% of registered voters cast ballots. In that election, 122,361 of St. Lucie County’s 238,645 registered voters voted. The county ranked 51st among Florida’s 67 counties, with 16 counties reporting lower turnout. Tuesday’s participation exceeded the county’s previous gubernatorial election turnout rate even as flooding disrupted access to some polling locations and required voters to cast ballots at alternate sites.

St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said the polling place changes were necessary to ensure voters had safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots. Voters assigned to Oak Hammock K-8 School, Centennial High School and the Paula A. Lewis Library were among those affected by the relocations. Some voters were redirected to the Port St. Lucie Community Center, Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence and Tradition Town Hall. The changes affected several polling places across the three communities as election officials responded to the flooding.

Heavy rainfall submerged roads, stranded vehicles and prompted evacuations across parts of St. Lucie County. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for the county and six other Florida counties. Flooding also forced local public schools to close Tuesday and Wednesday. Those conditions coincided with Election Day, when the county recorded both a higher turnout rate than in 2022 and a Democratic majority in the governor’s race.

The result marked the first time since 2012 that a Democratic candidate for governor or president won a majority in St. That year, former President Barack Obama carried the county with 53.42% of the vote. According to TCPalm , voter turnout reached 56.5% in the county, up 5.2 percentage points from the 2022 general election , when 51.3% of registered voters cast ballots. Lucie County ranked 51st among Florida's 67 counties, with only 16 counties reporting lower turnout. In 2022, the county had 238,645 registered voters, with 122,361 casting ballots. Voters assigned to Oak Hammock K-8 School, Centennial High School and the Paula A. Lewis Library were among those affected, with some redirected to the Port St. Lucie Community Center, Indian River State College's Veterans Center of Excellence and Tradition Town Hall. hero.headline: Jensen Beach flooding disrupts voting; Martin County under state of emergency
hero.body:
Flooding in Jensen Beach after days of heavy rain forced an Election Day precinct move, while Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency covering Martin County and six other counties. The Martin County Supervisor of Elections moved Precinct 2 due to flooding. Martin County Public Schools closed Tuesday.

On Sunday, the National Weather Service said radar indicated 2.5 to 4 inches of rain had fallen by 3:52 p.m. in Martin County and southeastern St. Lucie County. Jensen Beach was among the affected communities. Executive Order 26-227 says a broad area of low pressure brought widespread heavy rainfall across parts of Florida.

Martin County’s flood protection page warns that a typical homeowner’s insurance policy does not cover flood damage. The page also notes multiple instances of significant flooding affecting homeowners in low- to moderate-risk flood zones, designated Flood Zone X.
hero.article_text: Martin County’s flood protection page warns that the typical homeowner’s insurance policy does not include coverage for damage resulting from flooding, and that there have been multiple instances of homeowners in low- to moderate-risk flood zones (Flood Zone X) who have experienced significant flooding The flooding follows days of heavy rain across the Treasure Coast. On Sunday, the National Weather Service said radar indicated between 2.5 and 4 inches of rain had already fallen by 3:52 p.m. in Martin County and southeastern St. Lucie County, and listed Jensen Beach among the affected communities. Ron DeSantis signed Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency in Martin County and six other counties. The order says a broad area of low pressure brought widespread heavy rainfall across parts of Florida from Oct. Martin County Public Schools closed Tuesday, and the Martin County Supervisor of Elections moved Precinct 2 in Jensen Beach due to flooding for Election Day.

hero.headline: Florida special session expected to implement Amendment 3 homestead tax relief
hero.body:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said Wednesday that a special legislative session is expected to implement Amendment 3, the voter-approved measure expanding homestead property tax relief. The amendment must be implemented by Jan. 1. DeSantis said the legislation would set a schedule for further relief and seek to prevent local governments from offsetting homeowners’ savings with other taxes or fees.

DeSantis said he would work with legislative leaders to determine when lawmakers should return to Tallahassee before he leaves office in January. He wants lawmakers to establish what he called a “taxpayer bill of rights” and is considering state grants to help local governments cover essential services. That assistance could total tens of millions of dollars, particularly for rural communities facing funding shortfalls for core services such as sheriff’s departments, he said. “It's not going to be a tax shift,” DeSantis said. “It's going to be a reduction.”

Amendment 3 does not apply to school districts, and DeSantis said the implementing legislation would preserve that exemption. He suggested lawmakers could eventually revisit Florida’s education funding formula as they consider additional property tax relief for homeowners without reducing support for public schools. His ultimate goal is to move Florida closer to making homesteaded property tax-free, though he said that would require additional action after his term ends. “The more we can get the homestead to just be tax free, I think that's the better,” he said.

Speaking the day after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, DeSantis also credited Amendment 3 with helping Republicans withstand major Democratic gains elsewhere in the country. He argued that the measure drew voters who then supported Republican candidates further down the ballot. “Had Amendment 3 not been on the ballot, I don't know that we turn out the voters that we ended up turning out,” he said.

DeSantis described the national results as “close to an extinction-level event” for Republicans but said Florida’s results reflected voter trust in the party’s record during his two terms. He urged Republicans nationally to pay greater attention to economic concerns, including inflation, mortgage rates, gas prices, and grocery prices, rather than emphasizing issues he believed had been more effective in earlier elections.

cards.headline: St. Lucie County reports 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls
cards.body:
Emergency crews handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls amid widespread flooding in St. Lucie County, officials said Tuesday, as rescue operations continued and the county opened two shelters. Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and warned that floodwater could take several days to recede.

Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said crews received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period. County public safety director Ron Guerrero said estimated rainfall totals ranged from 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Flooding affected Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, areas around California and Peacock boulevards, and areas around Virginia Avenue. The Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Crews were assessing roads and infrastructure. They were also clearing drainage and roadways, though safety concerns limited some high-water operations after dark.

The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the time of the briefing, Guerrero said. The school district planned to keep schools closed Wednesday, Nov. 4, and hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, and the landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations.

Officials warned that road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents seeking relocated vehicles can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000. The city also warned of a one-day delay in solid waste collection, with pickups shifting to the next service day, including Saturday.

Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised avoiding standing water, especially with cuts or open wounds, and washing with soap and water after exposure. Residents should discard food or household items exposed to floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Flood-affected private wells should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

hero.headline: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin by 2,601 votes in Port St. Lucie mayoral race
hero.body:
Steven Giordano unseated Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin by 2,601 votes Tuesday, with all 62 precincts reporting. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and increasing transparency in city spending.

Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin’s 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Election-day, early and mail votes were marked completely reported as of 12:34 a.m.

During his campaign, Giordano argued that developers should pay their fair share of infrastructure improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as Port St. Lucie continues expanding. He called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion and sought to hold developers accountable for infrastructure improvements. He also called for an independent forensic audit of city spending and promised greater transparency at City Hall.

Martin defended her administration’s approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for a growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard at Savona Boulevard and Tradition Parkway at Village Parkway. Martin also pointed to 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city’s property tax rate.

The candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August’s three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%.

Port St. Lucie voters also rejected a proposal to pay an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly residential garbage collection. The latest election results showed 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The referendum was nonbinding, meaning the vote provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County moving flood shelters as Port St. Lucie flooding persists
hero.body:
St. Lucie County Emergency Management is moving its temporary flood shelters Wednesday morning to help St. Lucie public schools reopen, while significant standing water remains in parts of Port St. Lucie. Officials warn that water levels could take several days to recede as recovery efforts continue.

The general population shelter is moving from Northport K-8 School to the Havert L. Fenn Center in Fort Pierce. The special medical needs shelter is relocating from the Fenn Center. On Wednesday, 16 people were staying at the general population shelter and five at the special medical needs shelter. The county opened the shelters with St. Lucie Public Schools and the St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office to help residents displaced by this week’s flooding.

Water levels have receded in some areas, but significant standing water remains at several locations, including SW Cashmere Boulevard, Lake Forest HOA, St. Bernadette Church, NW Country Club Drive, Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard. Public works and water management agencies have opened water control structures, but recent heavy rainfall and King Tides are limiting where the water can drain.

Port St. Lucie Police Department officers continue to check on residents, monitor roadways and assist people affected by the flooding. City crews, partner agencies and community organizations are also supporting recovery efforts and working to restore normal conditions safely.

Officials urge residents to drive carefully, watch for flooded roads and never go around barricades or enter closed roadways. They also encourage residents to check on neighbors and loved ones who may need help. Updates on road closures and other services affected by flooding are available through the St. Lucie County Emergency Readiness Portal.

hero.headline: Steven Giordano defeats Shannon Martin to win Port St. Lucie mayoral race
hero.teaser: Giordano won by just over 2,400 votes, reversing a nearly 13-percentage-point deficit to Martin in the August primary.
hero.body:
Steven Giordano defeated incumbent Shannon Martin by just over 2,400 votes to win the race for Port St. Lucie mayor, reversing his nearly 13-percentage-point deficit in the August primary.

Giordano celebrated with supporters Tuesday night at Recovery Sports Grill in Tradition after pulling ahead with more than 51% of the vote. At his election-night watch party, he said he believed voters responded to his message and approach to the race.

“I think they saw somebody that was dedicated, that was here for all the right reasons,” Giordano said. “I think they watched the debate.”

Giordano said he wants to serve residents rather than approach the position as a politician. “I think they saw somebody who is here for all the right reasons, that's not a politician, that's not here for money, that's here to do the right thing for the people,” he said. “And I'm proud to be the people's mayor.”

The general election followed a contentious August primary that included an FDLE investigation involving campaign signs. The investigation led to Martin's husband and two other Port St. Lucie police officers being placed on paid administrative leave.

cards.body:
St. Lucie County emergency crews handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls amid widespread flooding, officials said Tuesday. Schools were set to remain closed Wednesday, Nov. 4. Officials warned that road conditions could change quickly and urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel. Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria said water could take several days to recede.

The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. Residents should call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Public Safety Director Ron Guerrero said dispatchers received nearly 4,000 calls Monday and more than 1,800 Tuesday. Call takers were screening requests to keep emergency vehicles available for urgent situations.

Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said the fire district received 518 calls for service over 36 hours. Guerrero estimated rainfall totals at 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Flooding affected Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area and Tradition, along with neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive. Areas around California Boulevard, Peacock Boulevard and Virginia Avenue also flooded.

The county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Crews continued high-water rescues, assessed roads and infrastructure, and worked to clear drainage and roadways. Guerrero said safety concerns limited some high-water operations after dark. The school district hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions.

Port St. Lucie residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000. The city also warned of a one-day solid waste collection delay, with service shifting to the next service day, including Saturday.

Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised avoiding standing water, especially with cuts or open wounds, and washing with soap and water after exposure. Residents should not eat or use food or household items that touched floodwater. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water or boil or disinfect it. Flood-affected private wells should be tested for bacteria before use resumes. Questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can be directed to 772-873-4931.

hero.headline: Flood-related polling relocations extend beyond Precinct 90 in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Flood-related Election Day polling changes in St. Lucie County extend beyond the relocation of Precinct 90 from Legacy High School to Tradition Town Hall. Election officials also designated replacement voting sites for precincts 49, 71, 51, 67, 86, 83, 92 and 12, with specific access routes for two locations.

The Supervisor of Elections Office announced the changes in a notice posted Monday. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to some voting sites. The office said the moves were intended to give voters safe and accessible locations to cast their ballots.

The notice directs voters in precincts 49 and 71, whose regular polling place is Oak Hammock K-8 School, to the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd. Precinct 51 voters, who normally vote at the Disabled American Veterans Hall, are also assigned to the community center. The county says voters should enter from Airoso Boulevard.

For precincts 67 and 86, the replacement polling place is Indian River State College’s Veterans Center of Excellence at 500 NW California Blvd., replacing Centennial High School. The county designates Peacock Boulevard as the access route.

In the Tradition area, Precinct 83 voters are directed from the Paula A. Lewis Library to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Ln. Precinct 92 voters, whose regular polling place is The Brennity at Tradition, are also assigned to Tradition Town Hall. That facility is also the replacement site for Precinct 90, where flooding and police roadblocks disrupted access to Legacy High School. The Precinct 90 relocation replaced earlier instructions to reach the school by an alternate route.

In Fort Pierce, the notice directs Precinct 12 voters from the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to the Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S US Highway 1.

Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov.

hero.headline: Steven Giordano unseats Shannon Martin as Port St. Lucie mayor by 2,601 votes
hero.body:
Steven Giordano defeated Port St. Lucie Mayor Shannon Martin by 2,601 votes Tuesday, with all 62 precincts reporting. Giordano campaigned on slowing growth, addressing traffic congestion and holding developers accountable for infrastructure improvements.

Giordano received 45,499 votes, or 51.47%, compared with Martin's 42,898 votes, or 48.53%. Election-day, early and mail voting results were marked complete as of 12:34 a.m.

Throughout the campaign, Giordano argued that developers should pay their fair share for infrastructure improvements, including sidewalks and streetlights, as Port St. Lucie continues expanding. He also called for a new traffic study to identify solutions to congestion. On city spending, Giordano called for an independent forensic audit and promised greater transparency at City Hall.

Martin defended her administration's approach to growth, arguing that while the city cannot stop people from moving to Port St. Lucie, it can plan for the growing population. She pointed to upcoming road improvements at major intersections, including Gatlin Boulevard at Savona Boulevard and Tradition Parkway at Village Parkway. On taxpayer spending, Martin cited 11 consecutive years of reductions in the city's property tax rate.

The candidates advanced to the November election after neither secured a majority in August's three-way primary. Martin finished first in August with 47.71% of the vote, followed by Giordano with 35.22% and Eric Strazzeri with 17.07%.

Port St. Lucie voters also rejected a proposal to pay an additional $131 per year for twice-weekly residential garbage collection. The results showed 71,181 voters, or 78.09%, voted no, while 19,971 voters, or 21.91%, voted yes. The nonbinding referendum provides guidance to city leaders rather than automatically changing trash collection services.

cards.teaser: The county opened a shelter at Northport K-8 School as crews responded to flooding. Officials urged residents to stay home if possible and reserve 911 for life-threatening emergencies.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County schools are closed Wednesday after flooding disrupted road access and left students walking through standing water to get home Monday. County leaders warned that conditions could take up to seven days to return to normal as emergency crews continued their flood response.

Superintendent Jon Prince said the district expects to reopen schools Thursday if roads are clear. During a Tuesday news conference, he apologized to families for the stress caused by Monday’s conditions and said the district had not anticipated the extent of the flooding.

The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals and coffee. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials asked residents to stay home if they can and call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies.

In the Tradition area, a private security company that patrols homeowners associations joined rescue efforts with high-water vehicles. TACT Tech Security CEO Taylor Matchton said his crews lifted elderly residents into a Jeep after water rose waist-high in one community. Matchton said the crews set out to help people wherever they could with the resources they had.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would work extra shifts overnight, especially in evacuated neighborhoods. He warned that anyone who preys on flood victims would face zero tolerance. Del Toro emphasized that responders were working together to serve the community.

Flooding also forced Election Day polling-place changes. Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker said inclement weather and flooding affected road access to voting sites. The changes included moving voting from Oak Hammock K-8 School and the Disabled American Veterans Hall to the Port St. Lucie Community Center, and from the Paula A. Lewis Library and The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall.

The county opened a general shelter at Northport K-8 School. Principal Brie Lamb said the campus stayed dry and has cots, blankets, meals, and coffee. Anybody who may need a place tonight, please come in, Lamb said. Officials said about 14 or 15 people were staying there at the time of the briefing. County leaders said it could take up to seven days for conditions to return to normal. The National Weather Service flood warning for St. Lucie County remains in effect until 9:30 a.m. Officials ask residents to stay home if they can and to call 911 only for life-threatening emergencies Voters with questions can call the Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 or visit stlucievotes.gov .

cards.headline: Fort Pierce restaurant owner promotes free books, renovates space for reading room
cards.teaser: Big Apple Pizza owner Scott Van Duzer is helping children get books mailed to their homes through New Worlds Reading while turning part of his restaurant into a reading room.
cards.body:
FORT PIERCE, Fla. Scott Van Duzer, owner of Big Apple Pizza, is working to connect children with free books mailed to their homes while renovating part of his restaurant into a reading room. He wants to expand access to books for children, especially those from low-income families.

Van Duzer has been involved with Read To Succeed, which he said has distributed 40,000 books over three years. He is now promoting New Worlds Reading as a way to get books to children more quickly. Van Duzer said signing up takes less than five minutes and children receive nine free books a year through fifth grade.

Amy York and her son Tripp read together using books he receives through New Worlds Reading. York described the program as a partnership with the University of Florida and Scholastic. “Well, it's awesome because they ship the books right to your house,” York said.

The reading room renovation is another part of Van Duzer’s effort to help children improve their reading. He emphasized the importance of giving children access to books early and keeping books in their homes. “It's just essential that we get books in kids' hands earlier and to have them in the home,” he said.
