hero.headline: Angie Nixon concedes Florida U.S. Senate special election to Ashley Moody
hero.body:
Democrat Angie Nixon conceded Florida’s U.S. Senate special election Tuesday after Republican Sen. Ashley Moody was projected to win, with votes still being counted.

Moody had just over 50% of the vote to Nixon’s approximately 48% as counting continued. Nixon, a Jacksonville Democrat and Florida state representative, had sought to become the state’s first Black U.S. senator.

In her concession speech, Nixon told supporters she would continue fighting for her progressive agenda. “We may have lost this battle, but the war is not over,” she said.

Nixon entered the general election after a surprise victory in the Democratic primary. Her campaign focused on affordability, with proposals including Medicare for All, free child care and rent freezes. Some supporters viewed the relatively close race as an opportunity for Democrats in a state where Republicans have built a substantial advantage.

Supporter Mak Manning praised Nixon’s grassroots campaign. “She's willing to get out there and into the streets and fight,” Manning said.

Nixon identified fundraising and closing the voter registration gap with Republicans as challenges facing Democrats. “That 1.5 million gap in registration, we need to fix that,” she said.

Asked about her next steps, Nixon said her immediate plans included getting some sleep. She also looked toward another election cycle: “I’m looking forward to 2028 because we’re getting to work,” she said.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County reports 120 flood rescues and water-related calls; schools closed Wednesday
hero.body:
St. Lucie County emergency crews had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls amid widespread flooding, county officials said Tuesday. Schools were set to remain closed Wednesday, with two shelters open and officials urging residents to avoid unnecessary travel as crews continued rescues and assessed roads.

Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said the fire district received 518 calls for service during a 36-hour period. County Public Safety Director Ron Guerrero said estimated rainfall totals ranged from 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Flooding affected Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition, neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive, and areas around California and Peacock boulevards, as well as Virginia Avenue.

The county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation. Crews were assessing roads and infrastructure while clearing drainage and roadways, Guerrero said. Some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns. Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria urged caution and said water could take several days to recede.

The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. Guerrero said about 14 or 15 people were staying in the shelters at the briefing. The school district hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. County offices and libraries were expected to reopen Wednesday, and the landfill was scheduled to resume normal operations.

Officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check the city’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents seeking relocated vehicles can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000. Solid waste collection was expected to run one day late, with collection days shifting to the next service day, including Saturday.

Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Sheriff Richard Del Toro said deputies would increase patrols, particularly in hard-hit areas and evacuated neighborhoods.

Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. He advised avoiding standing water, especially with cuts or open wounds, and washing with soap and water after exposure. Food and household items exposed to floodwater should not be used. Private wells affected by flooding should be tested for bacteria before use resumes.

The county’s public safety director, Ron Guerrero, said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Lucie County Schools Superintendent Dr. Prince apologized to families for the disruption caused when flooding affected school transportation Monday. He said district officials had been working with local agencies to get students and employees home safely. hero.headline: Flooding forces polling place moves in Fort Pierce and Port St. Lucie for Election Day
hero.body:
Flooding and unsafe road conditions forced temporary polling place relocations in Fort Pierce and Port St. Lucie for Tuesday’s election. St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker announced the changes Monday to give voters safe, accessible places to cast their ballots.

Election officials urged voters to verify their assigned polling locations before leaving home because additional changes may be necessary as flooding conditions evolve. Voters can check www.stlucievotes.gov or call the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 for updates.

The announced changes are:

• Precinct 12: Voting moved from Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge to Days Inn Midtown, the Precinct 25 location, at 3224 S. 1, Fort Pierce, FL 34982.

• Precincts 49 and 71: Voting moved from Oak Hammock K-8 School to Port St. Lucie Community Center, the Precinct 45 location, at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34984. Access is from Airoso Boulevard.

• Precinct 51: Voting moved from Disabled American Veterans Hall to Port St. Lucie Community Center, the Precinct 45 location, at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34984. Access is from Airoso Boulevard.

• Lucie West Centennial High School: Voting moved to Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence at 500 NW California Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34986. Access is from Peacock Boulevard.

• Lewis Library: Voting moved to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987.

• Precinct 92: Voting moved from The Brennity at Tradition to Tradition Town Hall at 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987.

The relocations followed days of heavy rainfall that flooded roads. Ron DeSantis issued Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties because of widespread flooding and threats to public safety and infrastructure.

St. Lucie County Sheriff Richard Del Toro urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and never attempt to drive through flooded roadways.

hero.headline: Rick Meltzer wins open Port St. Lucie City Council District 1 seat
hero.body:
Rick Meltzer won the open Port St. Lucie City Council District 1 seat, succeeding three-term Councilwoman Stephanie Morgan after campaigning on infrastructure-first growth and tighter spending oversight. With 58 of 62 precincts reporting, Meltzer had 56.7 percent of the vote to Idony Jean Baptist’s 43.3 percent. The district covers the city’s eastern and northeastern areas. Morgan did not seek reelection.

Meltzer, a mortgage loan originator and political newcomer, has lived in District 1 for more than 20 years. He has spent 17 years coaching and mentoring in youth sports. He says he would bring an outsider’s perspective to City Hall, with a platform focused on affordability, accountability and infrastructure. Meltzer led the four-candidate August primary with about 42 percent of the vote, followed by his opponent at about 22 percent. Neither reached the majority needed to win outright.

Meltzer says he would seek budget cuts and lower property taxes while holding contractors and developers to project deadlines and budgets. He wants road, utility and other infrastructure needs addressed before the city approves new development. He also opposes more zero-lot-line housing and supports building a sports complex. Meltzer has said he is researching the impacts of data centers, including water use, electricity demand and noise. He says their potential tax revenue and jobs could outweigh those concerns if the city protects residents’ interests.

Idony Jean Baptist is a minister and former Indian River County Sheriff’s Office detention deputy who ran for the same council seat in 2022 and later briefly filed to run for St. Lucie County sheriff before withdrawing. His campaign emphasized safer communities, transparent government, listening to residents, helping people in need and supporting small businesses. He proposed attracting more businesses to grow city revenue and reduce service costs for residents. He also supported moving to a double-can automated trash-pickup system, which he said could improve service and save money.

cards.headline: Troy Ingersoll wins sixth term on St. Lucie County School Board, defeating Lisa Kessler
cards.teaser: The School Board chairman won the District 5 runoff after Lisa Kessler narrowly led the August primary. Ingersoll identifies teacher staffing and rapid population growth as major challenges for the district.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County School Board Chairman Troy Ingersoll has secured a sixth term, defeating political newcomer Lisa Kessler in the District 5 runoff after a closely divided August primary. Ingersoll, who has served on the board since 2006, returns with priorities that include safe schools, stronger student achievement and responsible budgeting. He identifies teacher recruitment and retention, rapid population growth and leadership development as major challenges for the district’s next term.

Kessler narrowly led the August primary with 37.5% of the vote, compared with Ingersoll’s 37.2%, a difference of 167 votes. Charles Cerami received 25.2%. District 5 covers the eastern, coastal portion of the school district. School Board candidates must live in the districts they seek to represent, but all registered St. Lucie County voters were eligible to cast ballots in the nonpartisan race.

Ingersoll supports maintaining accelerated academic programs through consistent funding, targeted interventions and teacher development. He owns Pinch A Penny Pools and Spas in Vero Beach and serves as pastor of Midway Road Baptist Church. He holds a criminology degree from Florida State University and a master’s degree from New Orleans Baptist Theological Seminary.

Kessler campaigned on academic standards in reading, math, science and career readiness, along with recruiting and retaining qualified teachers. Her platform also emphasized stronger career and technical education, arts programs, better communication between schools and families, transparent budgeting and treating parents as partners in school decisions. She says public schools should make their case to families by highlighting certified teachers and programs unavailable elsewhere. A small-business owner, bestselling author and chair of the Fort Pierce Arts and Culture Advisory Board, Kessler spent 26 years in sales and marketing management before writing full time. Her campaign also highlighted her background as the daughter of two lifelong public-school teachers and her 11 years as a Girl Scout troop leader.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County reports 120 rescues and water-related calls; schools closed Wednesday
hero.body:
Emergency crews in St. Lucie County had handled 120 high-water rescues and water-related calls amid widespread flooding Tuesday, officials said. Schools will remain closed Wednesday, Nov. 4. Crews continued rescue operations, assessed roads and infrastructure, and worked to clear drainage and roadways. Public Safety Director Ron Guerrero said some high-water operations were limited after dark because of safety concerns.

The county opened a general population shelter at Northport K-8 School, 250 N.W. Floresta Drive in Port St. Lucie, and a special medical needs shelter at the Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. About 14 or 15 people were staying at the shelters at the time of the county briefing, Guerrero said. Officials urged residents to call 911 for life-threatening emergencies or immediate rescue needs. Interim County Administrator Mayté Santamaria urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and said water could take several days to recede.

Guerrero said officials estimated rainfall totals of 12 to 16 inches, with higher amounts in some areas. Flooding affected Creekside, the 10 Mile Creek area, Tradition and neighborhoods near Airoso Boulevard and Thornhill Drive. It also affected areas around California and Peacock boulevards, as well as Virginia Avenue. Interim Fire Chief Paul Langel said the fire district received 518 calls for service over 36 hours. The county’s Emergency Operations Center remained at a partial Level 2 activation.

The school district hoped to reopen Thursday, depending on road conditions. Officials said road closures and conditions could change quickly. Residents can check Port St. Lucie’s road closure map and report residential flooding through 1PSL. Vehicles obstructing roads or emergency response could be moved to a private tow yard or the MIDFLORIDA Event Center. Residents who believe their vehicle was relocated can call 1PSL at 772-871-1775 or the Port St. Lucie Police Department’s non-emergency line at 772-871-5000. The city also warned of a one-day solid waste collection delay, with collection shifting to the next service day, including Saturday.

Clint Sperber, the Florida Department of Health’s administrator and health officer for St. Lucie and Okeechobee counties, warned that floodwater can contain bacteria, viruses and other contaminants. Residents should avoid standing water, especially with cuts or open wounds, and wash with soap and water after exposure. Food and household items that touched floodwater should not be eaten or used. Anyone unsure whether tap water is safe should use bottled water, boil tap water or disinfect it. Flood-affected private wells should be tested for bacteria before use resumes. Questions about environmental health conditions at mobile home parks can be directed to 772-873-4931.

hero.headline: Roberts wins reelection to Martin County School Board District 1 with 60.14%
hero.body:
Christia Li Roberts won reelection to the Martin County School Board’s District 1 seat with 60.14% of the vote, defeating Cherie White, who received 39.86%. The nonpartisan contest returned the 12-year incumbent to the board. District 1 includes Hutchinson Island, Jensen Beach, North River Shores, Ocean Breeze Park, Rio and Sewall’s Point. Its schools and facilities include Jensen Beach High, Jensen Beach Elementary, Felix A. Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center.

Roberts’ priorities include preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028. She says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. Her campaign emphasized academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management. Roberts pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has generated additional operating revenue for schools. She also wants to improve student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction. Her goals include expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs.

A Stuart resident, Roberts has served on the School Board since 2014. She is a registered investment adviser and financial consultant with a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, she was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization supporting school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69%, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%.

White, a Jensen Beach resident, campaigned on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. White identified employee retention as an early priority, calling for fair pay, supportive work environments and stronger recruitment. She also proposed more campus-level decision-making, additional support for disadvantaged students and a plain-language budget with charts and visual data to help residents understand district spending.

Williams Elementary, Stuart Middle and the Environmental Studies Center. The contest was nonpartisan and pitted a 12-year incumbent against a challenger with local-government and classroom experience. Roberts finished first in the August primary with 49.69% of the vote, just short of the majority needed to win outright. White received 26.98%, and Charles Winn received 23.33%. Roberts , who lives in Stuart, has served on the School Board since 2014. She is also a registered investment adviser and financial consultant and has a bachelor’s degree in economics from Loyola University in Baltimore. In June, Roberts was named chair of the Florida School Labor Relations Service, a statewide organization that supports school districts in labor relations and collective bargaining. Roberts made her record on academic performance, safety, facilities and fiscal management central to her reelection campaign. She pointed to the district’s A rating, campus improvements, capital planning and referendum work that she says has produced additional operating revenue for schools. Her top priorities include improving student achievement through early intervention and personalized instruction; preparing to reauthorize the district’s operating referendum in 2028; and expanding STEM, career and technical education, arts and enrichment programs. Roberts says the referendum revenue supports teacher recruitment and retention, school safety, mental-health services and academic initiatives. On curriculum and library-material challenges, Roberts says the district should follow Florida law and School Board policy while maintaining transparent review procedures, public comment and parental opt-out options. She says individual parent concerns should be addressed without imposing unnecessary restrictions on other students. White , a Jensen Beach resident, brought a background in municipal government and education. She previously served as city clerk in Stuart, the first village clerk in Indiantown and town clerk in Sewall’s Point. She currently works for Martin County government and as a substitute teacher in Martin County schools. She has an elementary-education degree and a master municipal clerk credential. White said her experience as a parent of three, former local-government clerk and educator give her a practical understanding of how policy decisions affect students, families, school employees and budgets. Her campaign was centered on academic achievement, character development and stronger relationships among students, parents and teachers. White says the district should use targeted support to improve student outcomes, build more community engagement and provide families with clearer information about school decisions. White identified employee retention as an early priority. She said the district should provide fair pay, supportive work environments and a stronger recruitment process. She also has called for more decision-making at the campus level and for additional support for disadvantaged students, including mental-health resources, early-childhood interventions, family-engagement programs and school safety efforts. On school funding, White said she wants to protect well-funded neighborhood public schools as charter schools and private-school vouchers expand. She supports a legal, consistent process for curriculum and book challenges that respects diverse family values while preserving high-quality public education. White also proposed a plain-language budget with simpler explanations, charts and visual data so residents can better understand district spending. She says special-education reductions should not exceed the overall enrollment decline and that the district should seek state, federal and private grants to support students with disabilities.

hero.headline: Brian Mast wins reelection in Florida's 21st Congressional District
hero.body:
Republican Brian Mast won reelection Tuesday in Florida's 21st Congressional District, defeating Democratic challenger James Martin and securing another two-year term in the U.S. House of Representatives. The newly redrawn district includes portions of Palm Beach, Martin and St. Lucie counties.

Mast has served in Congress since 2017 and chairs the House Foreign Affairs Committee. Before entering politics, he served in the U.S. Army, losing both legs while serving in Afghanistan.

Martin, a U.S. Coast Guard veteran and former national security official in the Biden administration, won the Democratic primary in August. The general election field also included no-party-affiliation candidate Alexander Cooke and write-in candidate David Fabrikant.

hero.headline: Martin County schools weigh Wednesday operations after Tuesday flooding closure
hero.body:
The Martin County School District is evaluating weather-related damage and safety conditions before deciding whether classes will resume Wednesday, Nov. 4, following a Tuesday closure caused by severe flooding. Schools were closed Tuesday, Nov. 3, as flooding affected the Treasure Coast. The district said it would announce its Wednesday plans as soon as it finishes reviewing conditions. In its message, the district acknowledged that families and employees need to make arrangements around the school schedule. It said protecting students, staff and families remains its main concern as it determines whether schools can operate safely. The assessment will guide the district’s decision on Wednesday operations.

In neighboring St. Lucie County, school officials have announced that schools will remain closed Wednesday. Superintendent Dr. Prince announced the closure Tuesday after the district coordinated with local law enforcement and consulted the Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. The district expects schools to reopen Thursday, Nov. 5. Beyond the school closure, the district is helping with the response to flooding in the community. School resource officers are assisting with efforts on local roads, and a shelter has opened at one of the district’s school sites for families who have been displaced because their homes flooded.

Indian River County Public Schools and district locations will also stay closed Wednesday, Nov. 4, because flooded roads continue to make travel unsafe. Officials said assessments found district facilities operational, but transportation conditions remain a barrier to reopening. With 31 roads closed, school buses cannot run safely. The district hopes to reopen Thursday, Nov. Officials said they will continue coordinating with emergency management as they work toward reopening. Families and employees will receive updates through the district’s social media accounts and Live Feed as plans are confirmed. The Wednesday closure applies to both schools and district locations.

Okeechobee County schools, meanwhile, will reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, the district announced. The reopening follows work by crews to ensure schools and bus stops were safe and ready for students after the weather event. In announcing the return, the district thanked families and the broader community for their patience during those preparations. It also recognized the work of its operations, maintenance and custodial teams, along with school administrators and Okeechobee County Emergency Management. Okeechobee’s announcement confirms a Wednesday return, while Martin County continues its assessment and St. Lucie and Indian River counties keep schools closed that day.

hero.headline: Election Day flooding disrupts access to Legacy High School in Port St. Lucie
hero.body:
Flooding disrupted access to Legacy High School in Port St. Lucie on Tuesday, creating confusion for Precinct 90 voters as residents voted for the city’s next mayor. Voters assigned to the high school were being redirected to Precinct 89 at Tradition Town Hall, 10799 SW Civic Lane in Port St. Lucie. The change followed travel problems around the school, where flooding and police roadblocks had affected access earlier in the day. The updated direction for Precinct 90 voters was to go to Tradition Town Hall rather than continue to Legacy High School.

Earlier Tuesday, the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections had instructed voters to reach Legacy High School by taking Midway Road and Glade Extension. Flooding and roadblocks on Southwest Village Parkway prevented access from that direction, and police had closed that entrance to the campus. An alternate route initially allowed voters to reach the school despite the closure. The instructions changed from using another route to the high school to voting at a different location. Tradition Town Hall was also listed as the polling location for Precinct 92, which previously voted at The Brennity at Tradition.

Other polling location changes in St. Lucie County included Precinct 12, whose voters were directed to Days Inn Midtown at 3224 S. Highway 1 in Fort Pierce instead of the Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge. Voters in Precincts 49 and 71 were assigned to the Port St. Lucie Community Center at 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., replacing Oak Hammock K-8 School. Precinct 51 voters were also assigned to the community center, replacing the Disabled American Veterans Hall. Voters going to the community center were instructed to enter from Airoso Boulevard. The center was listed as the voting site for all three precincts.

The MIDFLORIDA Credit Union Event Center, 9221 SE Event Center Place in Port St. Lucie, was listed as the voting location for Precincts 67 and 86. Fenn Center at 2000 Virginia Ave. in Fort Pierce. Their previous polling location was Renaissance Business Park, formerly known as Orange Blossom Business Center. Paula A. Lewis Library remained open as a polling location.

hero.headline: Flooding forces Election Day polling-place moves in St. Lucie County

cards.teaser: Officials urge residents to travel only when necessary as numerous roads are flooded or impassable. Deputies and emergency personnel are coordinating with the Emergency Operations Center.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County public schools, county government offices and courthouses will be closed Tuesday as significant rainfall and flooding affect the area. County officials are urging residents to stay off the roads unless travel is necessary. Ron DeSantis issued Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties because of widespread flooding and threats to public safety and critical infrastructure.

The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office said numerous roads are flooded or impassable, with more rain expected through Monday night and Tuesday. The agency urged residents to stay home, never drive through floodwaters and avoid moving or driving around barricades and road-closure signs. Residents should stay away from downed power lines and standing water near electrical equipment, and monitor official sources for weather alerts and road updates. Deputies and other personnel remain on duty and are coordinating with the Emergency Operations Center. The sheriff’s office thanked deputies, dispatchers, emergency personnel and community partners responding to the conditions and urged residents to look out for their neighbors.

Flooding also has affected road access to some polling locations, prompting the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections to announce temporary polling-place changes for the Nov. 3 General Election. hero.body:
The Martin County School District is assessing flooding impacts and travel safety before deciding whether schools will reopen Wednesday, Nov. 4, following Tuesday’s closure. The Wednesday decision remains pending as the district reviews conditions after severe flooding along the Treasure Coast.

The district said it will announce Wednesday’s schedule as soon as possible after completing its assessment. It acknowledged that families and employees are making plans and said the safety and well-being of students, staff and families remain its priority. Martin County schools closed Tuesday, Nov. 3, because of flooding.

The St. Lucie County School District announced Tuesday that its schools will remain closed Wednesday. The decision was made in collaboration with local law enforcement and in consultation with the Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. The district anticipates reopening Thursday, Nov. 5. School resource officers are supporting efforts on local roadways, and the district has opened a shelter at one of its school sites for families displaced by flooded homes.

Indian River County Public Schools and district locations also will remain closed Wednesday because flooding continues to make travel unsafe. Officials said district facilities have been assessed and are operational, but 31 roads are closed and conditions prevent school buses from operating safely. The district hopes to reopen Thursday, Nov. 5, and continues to work with emergency management officials. It will share updates through its social media channels and Live Feed as reopening plans are confirmed.

hero.headline: St. Lucie Public Schools to close Wednesday after flooding, expects Thursday reopening
hero.body:
St. Lucie Public Schools will be closed Wednesday, Nov. 4, following severe flooding, with schools expected to reopen Thursday, Nov. 5, Superintendent Dr. Jon R. Prince announced. The district has also opened a shelter at one of its school sites for families displaced by flooded homes.

Prince said the closure decision was made in collaboration with local law enforcement and in consultation with the Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service. School resource officers will support efforts on local roadways. He urged families and employees to stay off flooded roads and take care of one another.

Prince also addressed his decision to keep schools open Monday, saying it was based on information received from the Emergency Operations Center and the National Weather Service on Sunday evening and early Monday morning. He said Martin, Indian River and St. Lucie proceeded as normal, as did local governmental agencies. Prince described the flooding as an unpredicted, unprecedented event. As rain continued Monday, the district called bus drivers to report early and asked parents to leave work to pick up or meet their children. He said the district recognizes the difficulty of sudden changes for families and seeks to avoid putting children and families on roads during the height of a storm.

“To our families and employees, I offer my sincerest apologies for the stress you experienced as the day progressed,” Prince said. He thanked teachers and staff who stayed to care for students, bus drivers who came in early and stayed late to get students home, and security teams who drove students and employees home after hours.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie tests flood sensors as Oak Hammock drainage project could take years
cards.teaser: The city is testing water-level sensors and clearing drainage systems as heavy rain strands drivers. Planned improvements in Oak Hammock remain in the data-collection phase.
cards.body:
Port St. Lucie is testing water-level sensors and clearing drainage systems as heavy rain floods roads and strands drivers, while a longer-term drainage project in the Oak Hammock neighborhood could take years to complete. The city says that project remains in the data-collection phase.

Plans for Oak Hammock include new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raising portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard to help address recurring flooding. In the meantime, the city says it is testing sensors to help crews respond more quickly to flooding and working to remove debris from drainage systems. Crews are also checking systems for water flow and addressing potholes reported or discovered during inspections.

Along Southwest Airoso Boulevard, floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep in some areas and covered sidewalks. Vehicles stalled as drivers attempted to pass through the water, leaving them waiting for help while passing cars sent waves toward stranded vehicles. Port St. Lucie police say officers are responding to a significant number of calls involving vehicles stranded in floodwaters.

The flooding also disrupted school pickups. One woman was trying to figure out how to retrieve her children after parents were notified to pick up their students. She said her sister lost a nearly new vehicle to flooding on the same road last year and questioned whether the city's road expansion efforts were being matched with drainage improvements. Another driver said his vehicle stopped working while he was trying to pick up his children.

Port St. Lucie police are asking residents to stay home and avoid travel unless absolutely necessary. Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and urge drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

cards.headline: Flooded Port St. Lucie roads remain hazardous as crews check Creekside homes
cards.teaser: SW Rosser Road at SW Paar Drive and SW Delos Drive remained flooded and impassable Tuesday morning. Emergency crews were checking homes in Creekside as police monitored roads across Port St. Lucie.
cards.body:
Flooded roads remained hazardous across Port St. Lucie on Tuesday morning, with SW Rosser Road at SW Paar Drive and SW Delos Drive still impassable as water receded elsewhere. The St. Lucie County Sheriff’s Office drone team was working with the St. Lucie County Fire District to conduct home checks in the Creekside community.

Police reported flooding or barricades at Port St. Lucie Boulevard at Aviation Avenue; northbound Port St. Lucie Boulevard from Dalton Boulevard to Gatlin Boulevard; Selvitz Road from Midway Road to Peachtree Boulevard; and Peachtree Boulevard. Other affected locations included Westmoreland Boulevard in front of The Anchorage, Savona Boulevard and California Boulevard, St. Lucie West Boulevard, Volusia Drive from Blanton Boulevard to Torino Parkway, California Boulevard in front of Fire Station 14, Country Club Estates of St. Lucie West and northbound Cashmere Boulevard.

Aerial footage shared by police showed significant flooding near SW Savage Boulevard, SW Fairgreen Road and SW Salvatierra Boulevard, with water spread across residential streets and surrounding areas. Flooding also affected roads and neighborhoods near Tradition Parkway and SW Community Boulevard, as well as Torino Parkway, NW California Boulevard and NW Peacock Boulevard. Police said standing water made travel hazardous in those areas.

Water was beginning to recede on Lennard Road at Melaleuca Boulevard, Hillmoor Drive in front of HCA St. Lucie Medical Center and near the 1700 block, and Village Green Drive. Vehicles could pass on those roads, police said, though four disabled vehicles on Lennard Road awaited removal.

Flooding had subsided on Becker Road from Hallmark Street to Savona Boulevard, Darwin Boulevard and College Park Road. Several disabled vehicles remained on Becker and Darwin. Water had also cleared on Darwin Boulevard at Fifer Avenue, where two disabled vehicles remained. Rosser Boulevard had cleared, while the intersections on SW Rosser Road remained flooded and impassable.

Police extended patrol shifts overnight to keep additional officers available for emergencies. Officers assessed roads and neighborhoods at daybreak, helped stranded motorists, responded to calls and monitored flooding throughout the city.

Police urged residents to stay home unless travel was necessary, avoid flooded roads and never drive through standing water. The department cautioned that conditions could change quickly, especially with more rain. Residents should call 911 to report downed power lines, fallen trees, road obstructions or other hazards posing an immediate danger.

cards.headline: Legacy High School polling site remains open amid Port St. Lucie flooding
cards.teaser: Precinct 90 voters should take Midway Road and Glade Extension to reach the school. Voters unable to get there can obtain a vote-by-mail ballot at the elections office’s Tradition office.
cards.body:
Precinct 90 at Legacy High School in Port St. Lucie remains open for voting Tuesday despite flooding and road closures that have made the polling location difficult to reach, the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections office confirmed. The office is directing voters to take Midway Road and Glade Extension to the school. Flooding and roadblocks affected Southwest Village Parkway earlier Tuesday, and police blocked that entrance. Voters could still reach the school by the alternate route. Port St. Lucie voters are choosing the city’s next mayor Tuesday.

Voters who cannot reach Legacy High School can go to the elections office’s Tradition office at 10-267 Southwest Village Parkway, where election staff can print a vote-by-mail ballot. Voters can complete and sign the ballot, then return it as directed by staff, the elections office said. That option is separate from voting at Tradition Town Hall, which is the assigned polling location for Precinct 92.

Flooding and changing information about the polling location caused confusion for some voters. Tommy Sharpe said he was directed to Tradition Town Hall but was told he could not vote there because it was not his assigned precinct. He said he was then told Legacy High School was open and he would need to take a back route. Sharpe said the detour would add 20 to 35 minutes to his drive. Tradition Town Hall is at 10799 SW Civic Lane and replaced The Brennity at Tradition as Precinct 92’s polling location.

Other St. Lucie County polling locations include the Port St. Lucie Community Center, 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., for precincts 49, 51 and 71, with access from Airoso Boulevard. Precincts 49 and 71 previously voted at Oak Hammock K-8 School, while Precinct 51 previously used Disabled American Veterans Hall. Precincts 85 and 95 are assigned to the MIDFLORIDA Credit Union Event Center, 9221 SE Event Center Place, replacing Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence. Precinct 12 is at Days Inn Midtown, 3224 S. Highway 1 in Fort Pierce, replacing Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge. Precincts 6 and 28 are at Havert L. Fenn Center, 2000 Virginia Ave. in Fort Pierce, replacing Renaissance Business Park, formerly Orange Blossom Business Center. Paula A. Lewis Library also remains open as a polling location.

hero.headline: St. Lucie County, Port St. Lucie declare flood emergencies as county activates response center
hero.body:
St. Lucie County and the City of Port St. Lucie declared local states of emergency Monday as flooding affected streets and neighborhoods. The county’s Emergency Operations Center is operating under a Level 2 partial activation, with Public Safety personnel coordinating the response with law enforcement, water management agencies and local governments. County officials said the declaration would expedite access to additional resources that may be needed.

Crews are working to address flooding problems across St. Lucie County. Officials urged residents to refrain from traveling Monday evening if possible and warned motorists against driving through flooded roads. Port St. Lucie issued its emergency declaration in alignment with the county. The City Council was scheduled to meet Tuesday at 1 p.m. at City Hall to vote to formally approve the State of Emergency, which can help expedite additional resources as needed.

The Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County warned residents about health hazards associated with floodwaters. Health officials advise people to avoid contact with floodwater, particularly if they have open cuts or sores, and not to eat or drink anything contaminated by it. Anyone whose wounds have been exposed to floodwater should thoroughly wash the affected area with soap and seek medical care if redness, swelling or drainage develops.

Heavy rainfall could also make water from flooded private wells unsafe to drink, health officials said. Residents who are unsure whether flooding has affected their wells should use bottled or boiled water for drinking, making ice, brushing their teeth and cleaning cuts or injuries. People whose septic systems are experiencing slow plumbing should conserve water and avoid having their septic tanks pumped while groundwater levels remain exceptionally high.

Indian River County also declared a local state of emergency Monday, citing ongoing flooding, deteriorating weather and continued rainfall. County officials said numerous roads had become impassable. The county urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel through flood-affected areas, obey road closures and barricades, and never drive through flooded roadways. Both counties asked residents to continue monitoring official sources as conditions change.

cards.headline: Knee-deep flooding strands drivers on Southwest Airoso Boulevard in Port St. Lucie
cards.teaser: Police urge residents to avoid unnecessary travel as floodwaters stall vehicles. The city's Oak Hammock drainage project remains in data collection and could take years to complete.
cards.body:
Heavy rain left drivers stranded on Southwest Airoso Boulevard in Port St. Lucie, where floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep in some areas and covered sidewalks. Vehicles stalled as drivers tried to cross the water, and passing traffic sent waves toward stranded cars. Port St. Lucie police said officers were responding to a significant number of calls involving vehicles stranded in floodwaters and urged residents to avoid travel unless absolutely necessary.

One driver said his vehicle died while he was trying to pick up his children, leaving him waiting for help from his insurance company. The man, who has lived in the area for six years, said he believes drainage conditions have worsened following heavy rain. Another woman's vehicle stopped working minutes after she drove toward Southwest Airoso Boulevard. Water rushed toward her vehicle, and a nearby man tried to help her get out. A couple stranded for about an hour described watching their vehicle sink deeper as waves from passing traffic pushed it around.

The flooding also complicated school pickups. One woman said parents had been notified to retrieve their children, leaving her trying to figure out how to reach them. She said her sister lost a nearly new vehicle to flooding on the same road last year. The vehicle was only three months old, she said. The woman questioned whether the city's road-widening work was being matched by drainage improvements.

The city says it is working on longer-term drainage improvements, including a project in the Oak Hammock neighborhood. Plans call for new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raising portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard to address recurring flooding. The project remains in the data-collection phase and could take years to complete.

In the meantime, the city says it is testing water-level sensors to help crews respond more quickly to flooding and clearing debris from drainage systems. Crews are checking drainage systems for water flow and addressing potholes reported or discovered during inspections.

Police are asking residents to stay home unless travel is absolutely necessary. Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and urge drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

hero.headline: Flooding covers Vero Beach neighborhood roads as deputies warn drivers to stay away
hero.body:
Heavy rain flooded roads, front lawns and driveways in several Vero Beach neighborhoods Monday, prompting deputies to urge residents to stay off roads and avoid driving through floodwaters. Deputies warned that conditions remained unsafe after rounds of rain moved through the area.

Water covered streets and properties along 41st Avenue and 12th Street, about a mile from Glendale Elementary School. Neighbors said they had never seen flooding this severe in the area. Residents said steady rain throughout the day overwhelmed drainage systems, sending water into neighborhood streets and yards.

A photo shared by the sheriff's office showed only the roof of an SUV above the floodwaters at one point. Residents continued waiting for the water to recede.

The scene along 41st Avenue and 12th Street, about a mile from Glendale Elementary School, showed water covering roads, front lawns and driveways. Neighbors said they have never seen flooding this severe in the area before. Residents say the steady rain throughout the day overwhelmed drainage systems, leaving water with nowhere to go but into neighborhood streets and yards. A photo shared by the sheriff's office showed just how high the water rose at one point, with only the roof of an SUV visible above the floodwaters. cards.headline: St. Lucie County declares flooding emergency; Port St. Lucie schedules Tuesday vote
cards.teaser: St. Lucie County's Emergency Operations Center is under a Level 2 partial activation. Health officials are warning residents about floodwater exposure and potentially unsafe private-well water.
cards.body:
St. Lucie County declared a local state of emergency Monday afternoon as flooding affected streets and neighborhoods, a step intended to expedite access to additional resources. The City of Port St. Lucie also declared an emergency, with the City Council scheduled to vote Tuesday at 1 p.m. at City Hall to formally approve it.

The county's Emergency Operations Center is operating under a Level 2 partial activation. Public Safety personnel are coordinating with law enforcement, water management agencies and local governments in response to the flooding. Crews are working to address problems across the county. Officials urged residents to avoid travel Monday evening if possible and warned motorists against attempting to drive through flooded roads. Port St. Lucie's declaration aligns with the county's and can help expedite additional resources as needed.

The Florida Department of Health in St. Lucie County is warning residents about potential health hazards associated with floodwaters. Residents should avoid eating or drinking anything contaminated with floodwater and avoid contact with floodwater, particularly if they have open cuts or sores. Anyone whose wounds have been exposed should thoroughly wash the affected area with soap and seek medical care if redness, swelling or drainage develops.

Health officials also warned that heavy rainfall could make water from flooded private wells unsafe to drink. Residents unsure whether flooding has affected their well should use bottled or boiled water for drinking, making ice, brushing their teeth and cleaning cuts or injuries. People with septic systems experiencing slow plumbing should conserve water and avoid having their septic tanks pumped while groundwater levels remain exceptionally high. County officials are asking residents to continue monitoring official sources as conditions change.

cards.headline: Flooding strands Port St. Lucie drivers as Oak Hammock drainage project could take years
cards.teaser: Floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep along parts of Southwest Airoso Boulevard. The city says it is testing water-level sensors and clearing drainage systems while planning longer-term improvements.
cards.body:
Heavy rain stranded drivers in Port St. Lucie as floodwaters reached approximately knee-deep along parts of Southwest Airoso Boulevard, while a city drainage project aimed at recurring flooding in Oak Hammock remains in the data-collection phase. The city says that project could take years to complete. Police are responding to a significant number of calls involving stranded vehicles and urging residents to avoid travel unless absolutely necessary.

Along Southwest Airoso Boulevard, water covered sidewalks and stalled vehicles whose drivers attempted to cross flooded stretches. Passing cars sent waves toward vehicles already stuck. One man said his vehicle died while he was trying to pick up his children. “I'm on hold with the insurance company right now trying to get some help,” he said. The man, who has lived in the area for six years, said he believes drainage conditions have worsened following heavy rain events.

Another driver became stranded after her vehicle stopped working just minutes after she drove toward Southwest Airoso Boulevard. “Every time a car comes by, it pushes my car,” she said. Water continued rushing toward her vehicle, and a nearby man eventually tried to help her get out. A couple nearby described watching their vehicle sink deeper into the floodwaters after being stranded for about an hour, with passing traffic pushing waves against the car.

The flooding also complicated school pickups. One woman said she was trying to figure out how to retrieve her children after parents were notified to pick up their students. She said her sister lost a nearly new vehicle to flooding on the same road last year and questioned whether the city's road widening efforts were being matched with drainage improvements.

The city's Oak Hammock plans include new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raising portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard to help address recurring flooding. In the meantime, the city says it is testing water-level sensors to help crews respond more quickly and clearing debris from drainage systems. Crews are also checking drainage systems for water flow and addressing potholes reported or discovered during inspections.

Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and urge drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

hero.headline: Martin County district schools closed Tuesday, after-school activities canceled
hero.body:
All Martin County School District-operated schools will be closed Tuesday, Nov. 3, and all after-school activities are canceled as flooding and severe weather create unsafe travel conditions. District officials said the decision took into account the safety of students, families and employees, including those who commute into Martin County from neighboring communities.

Conditions vary significantly across the region, with some communities experiencing serious flooding and difficult travel, school officials said in a Facebook post. Throughout Monday, the district received reports of employees and families driving through floodwaters to get home, abandoning vehicles because roads were impassable and making alternate overnight accommodations because they could not safely remain in their homes. The district said many employees and families live outside Martin County, and conditions in those neighboring communities played an important role in the closure decision.

Officials also considered whether employees could safely travel to and from campuses and whether schools would have enough staff and resources to support students safely throughout the day. The district said the closure follows Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis' declaration of a state of emergency covering Martin County and surrounding counties. “We encourage everyone to use caution and prioritize their safety as conditions continue to affect our region,” the district said. Families are asked to monitor the Martin County School District's website and social media accounts for updates.

Okeechobee County schools also will remain closed Tuesday. District officials announced Monday evening that lingering floodwaters continued to prevent safe access to some campuses and had created unsafe conditions at several school bus waiting areas. Crews assessed campuses and access routes Monday, and officials consulted with the Okeechobee County Emergency Operations Center before deciding to keep schools closed. District teams will continue checking conditions Tuesday and provide updates about reopening. Officials also plan to announce in the coming days whether makeup days will be necessary.

hero.headline: Flooding strands Port St. Lucie drivers as police urge residents to stay off roads
hero.body:
Heavy rain has stranded drivers on flooded Port St. Lucie roads, prompting police to urge residents to stay home unless travel is absolutely necessary. Along Southwest Airoso Boulevard, water reached approximately knee-deep in some areas, covered sidewalks and stalled vehicles. Police say officers are responding to a significant number of calls involving stranded vehicles. Officials warn that even a few inches of moving water can be dangerous and urge drivers never to underestimate the depth or current of floodwaters.

Drivers caught in the flooding waited for help as passing traffic sent waves toward their vehicles. One man said his vehicle died while he was trying to pick up his children, leaving him seeking help from his insurance company. Another driver became stranded minutes after heading toward Southwest Airoso Boulevard. Water rushed toward her vehicle, and passing cars pushed it around. A nearby man eventually tried to help her get out. A couple also described watching their vehicle sink deeper into floodwaters after they had been stranded for about an hour.

The flooding also complicated school pickups and renewed residents’ concerns about drainage. One woman said she was trying to figure out how to retrieve her children after parents were notified to pick up their students. She said her sister had lost a vehicle that was only three months old to flooding on the same road last year. The woman questioned whether the city’s road widening efforts were being matched by drainage improvements. The man seeking insurance help said he had lived in the area for six years and believed drainage conditions had worsened following heavy rain.

The city says longer-term drainage improvements include a project in the Oak Hammock neighborhood, with plans for new retention ponds, drainage boxes and raised portions of California Boulevard and Savona Boulevard. That project remains in the data-collection phase and could take years to complete. In the meantime, the city says it is testing water-level sensors to help crews respond faster to flooding and clearing debris from drainage systems. Crews are also checking drainage systems for water flow and addressing potholes reported or found during inspections.

hero.headline: Flooding forces Election Day polling place relocations in St. Lucie County
hero.body:
Several Election Day polling locations in St. Lucie County have been temporarily relocated for Tuesday’s election because of flooding and unsafe road conditions. Election officials are urging voters to verify their assigned polling places before leaving home, as additional changes may be necessary as flooding conditions evolve.

Supervisor of Elections Gertrude Walker announced the relocations Monday, saying they are intended to give voters safe, accessible places to cast their ballots. Voters can check www.stlucievotes.gov or call the St. Lucie County Supervisor of Elections Office at 772-462-1500 for the latest updates.

The polling place changes are:

• Precinct 12, Fort Pierce Masonic Lodge: Voting has moved to Days Inn Midtown (Precinct 25), 3224 S. 1, Fort Pierce, FL 34982.

• Precincts 49 and 71, Oak Hammock K-8 School: Voting has moved to Port St. Lucie Community Center (Precinct 45), 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34984. Access is from Airoso Boulevard.

• Precinct 51, Disabled American Veterans Hall: Voting has moved to Port St. Lucie Community Center (Precinct 45), 2195 SE Airoso Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34984. Access is from Airoso Boulevard.

• Lucie West Centennial High School: Voting has moved to Indian River State College Veterans Center of Excellence, 500 NW California Blvd., Port St. Lucie, FL 34986. Access is from Peacock Boulevard.

• Lewis Library: Voting has moved to Tradition Town Hall, 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987.

• Precinct 92, The Brennity at Tradition: Voting has moved to Tradition Town Hall, 10799 SW Civic Lane, Port St. Lucie, FL 34987.

The relocations follow heavy rainfall and widespread flooding. Ron DeSantis issued Executive Order 26-227, declaring a state of emergency for St. Lucie County and six other Florida counties because of flooding and threats to public safety and infrastructure.

Sheriff Richard Del Toro urged residents to avoid unnecessary travel and never attempt to drive through flooded roadways.
